speechtext: LOGAN (Cumberland) moved that the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway Company be permitted to lay before the House their petition for the passing of an Act to authorize them to issue bonds, notwithstanding the expiration of the time for the presenting of petitions for Private Bills.

maintopic: TORONTO, HAMILTON AND BUFFALO RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: Explain.

maintopic: TORONTO, HAMILTON AND BUFFALO RAILWAY COMPANY.
speechtext: The Bill is to get leave to issue guaranteed bonds for the purpose of liquidating the obligations of the Toronto, Hamilton and Buffalo Railway Company. The reason it was not presented before is because the company were not in a position to liquidate with their creditors, many of whom are workingmen and contractors, when the time for presenting petitions in the regular way had expired. They are now in this position. The company are assuming certain liabilities of the contractors for debts due to workingmen and for material furnished, but as the bonding power of the company is exhausted, it is necessary to get permission to issue new bonds.

Motion agreed to.

The MINISTER OF JUSTICE (Hon. Charles Fitzpatrick) moved that the House go into committtee to-morrow to consider the following proposed resolution
Resolved, that it is expedient to amend the Supreme and Exchequer Court Acts, the Exchequer Court Act, and the Act respecting the Judges of Provincial Courts, and to provide as follows :-
1.	If any judge of the Supreme Court of Canada, or of the Exchequer Court of Canada, or of any Superior Court in Canada, resigns his office, His Majesty may, by letters patent, under the great seal, reciting such judge's age and period of service, grant unto him an annuity equal to the salary of the office held by him at the time of his resignation ; to commence immediately after his resignation, and to continue thenceforth during his natural life, provided such judge has (a) attained the age of seventy-five years, and continued in office as judge of one or more of the said courts, or as such judge, and as stipendiary magistrate ot the North-west Territories, for twenty years or upwards ; or (b) attained the age of seventy years and continued in office as judge of one or more of the said courts for twenty-five years or upwards ; or (c) continued in office as judge of one or more of the said courts for thirty years or upwards.
2.	Every County Court judge who has attained the age of seventy-five years shall be compulsorily retired ; and His Majesty may, by letters patent, under the great seal, reciting such judge's age and period of service, grant unto him an annuity, if he has continued in office as such judge for twenty-five years or upwards, equal to the salary of the office held by him at the time of his retirement ; or if he has continued in office as such judge for a less period, equal to two-thirds of such salary ; the said annuity to commence immediately after his retirement, and to continue thenceforth during his natural life.
His Excellency the Governor General has taken cognizance of this resolution and recommends it to our approval.
Motion agreed to.

Resolved, that it be expedient to provide as follows : -
1. The Governor in Council may from time to time advance and pay to the corporation of the

Harbour Commissioners of Montreal (hereinafter called 'the corporation'), in addition to the moneys authorized to be advanced to the corporation by the Governor in Council by chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session), and by chapter 47 of the statutes of 1898, and by chapter 9 of the Statutes of 1901, such sums of money, not exceeding in the whole the sum of three million dollars, as are required to enable the corporation to construct such further terminal facilities as are necessary property to equip the port of Montreal.
2.	No such advances shall be made unless the plans, specifications and estimates for the works to be performed by the corporation, and on which the money so to be advanced is to be expended, have first been submitted to and approved by the Governor in Council.
3.	The corporation shall, upon any advance being made, deposit with the Minister of Finance and Receiver General debentures of the corporation equal to par vaiue to the advance so made (which debentures the corporation are hereby authorized to issue), and such debentures so issued shall be of such amounts as the Minister of Finance and Receiver General determines, and shall bear date on the day when such advance is made, and shall be repayable within twenty-five years from the date of their issue, and in the meantime shall bear interest at the rate of three per cent per annum, such interest to be payable half yearly on the first day of July and the first day of January in each year.
4.	The principal and interest of the sums advanced under the authority of this Act to the corporation shall be paid by the corporatico out of its revenue mentioned in section 8 of chapter 10 of the statutes of 1896 (first session), and shall be a charge upon the said revenue in the same manner and to the same extent as if the sums so advanced had been borrowied by the corporation under the said chapter 10.
Motion agreed to.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. I. TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
speechtext: I would like to inquire from the right hon. the leader of the House when it would be convenient for him that I should take up the motion of which I gave notice some time ago. Of course, I quite understand that the motion of my hon. friend the leader of the opposition should take precedence, but after that motion has been disposed of, I would like very much that the right hon. gentleman would inform the House when it would be convenient for him to take up mine.
If convenient to my hon. friend, we will be ready to take up his motion on Thursday next.
The MINISTER OF FINANCE (Hon. W. S. Fielding) moved that the House again go into Committee of Supply.
['The Railway Bill will be taken up in the afternoon, and supply later.']

Some days ago, Mr. Speaker. I gave notice to the House that when my hon. friend the Minister of Finance would again move the House into Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
Committee of Supply I would move an amendment, the terms of which I then stated. As some observations have been made in the public press with regard to the time at which that motion was introduced, I would like to say, in the first place, that it was introduced in pursuance of a policy decided on several weeks ago, and so decided upon, not with respect to a single resolution, but with respect to several resolutions which was proposed on this side to 'bring to the attention of the House and the country. There is no - doubt whatever, I think, that the iron industry is a very important one to any country which possesses the proper resources and material for developing it. Every one of the foremost countries in the civilized world possessing resources for the manufacture of iron and iron products has, either first or last, given that industry such protection as has resulted in its development. It is quite true that, so far as the mother country is concerned, the policy of free trade has prevailed there since 1S47 in relation to the iron industry. But we must remember that that industry had obtained a very firm footing in Great Britain under a protective tariff long before the era of free trade in that country.
The iron industry is important because it affords the materials useful and necessary to the development of every country in the* world. It is an important industry also on account of the large number of men it employs, and because it lays the foundation for many other industries. For these reasons, therefore, Canada, it seems to me, possessing the resources and the raw material necessary for the development of this industry, ought to give it such protection as will enable us to utilize to the fullest possible extent those raw materials, those resources, with which Providence has blessed us and which it is our duty, as inheritors of this country to utilize. It may not be out of place to remind the House that Canada possesses, not in one place, but in many places, all the materials which are necessary for the manufacture of iron and steel. We possess the means of economically assembling these materials at the seaboard in the province of Nova Scotia, and also we possess the means of so assembling them on the shores of our great inland waters. And, although the iron industry in Canada has not always in times past been the success that we could desire it to have been, it seems to me, that there is no reason why it could' not be made a success. And in that view, I think, I am supported by the language, to which I will call attention in a few minutes, of my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) both in 1807 and in 1899, when certain legislation was enacted with regard to this industry.
A writer who paid great attention to this question, and who was interested in

the iron trade to some considerable extent in days gone by in Canada, has spoken of the resources of this country and of the possibility of building up our great iron industry. I will refer to the work of Mr. J. H. Bartlett, published in 1885, after a pretty thorough investigation by him of the practicability of carrying on the manufacture of iron successfully in this country. He says
Again, as respects the second of the Baconian conditions to national prosperity, the possession of ' busy workshops,' Canada, more especially since the development of the national policy, has, in a general sense, made great advances. There is, though, one special branch of industry, wherein she has, to a degree almost painfully surprising, failed to attain any appreciable rank among the nations, and wherein she has indeed Icing lagged, and still lags, far behind in the march of material progress. We refer, of course, to that great industry, so valued by other nations when endowed by nature with the means of cultivating it, the manufacture of iron. If, under the dispensation of Providence, the successful and profitable manufacture of iron in Canada -was an impossibility or even a dangerous or difficult venture, we would be compelled philosophically ,to accept the position. Just as we all of us, with repining, submit to the veto of nature against the cultivation, on our lands, of sago, tea or oranges. Nature, however, most assuredly, has not placed any such veto oh the manufacture of iron in our Dominion, hut, on the contrary, has, in certain portions of our domain, most bountifully endowed us with all the essentials to the successful operation of this great industry. It is we ourselves who, through our apathy, want of knowledge, or through defective legislation, have so long failed, and are still failing, to duly recognize the immense possibilities which lie within our easy reach, but which, in our blindness, we fail to grasp and 'develop as we should do.
The relation of the various attempts to make iron in this country presents a sad record of loss and disappointment, of blasted hopes and shattered fortunes. These enterprises appear generally to have been undertaken by men of energy and ability,

but, unable to make headway against the competition of older countries, they had, one after another, to succumb.
Now, my hon. friend the Minister of Finance, in speaking in 1897 upon the changes which were then made in the tariff, used the following language as appears in ' Hansard ' of that year, page 1,130
How far it was a wise policy to undertake the development of the iron industry in Canada in the way the hon. gentleman (Sir Charles Topper) attempted, in the face of many difficulties, and in the light of our experience how far that was a wise policy may well admit of argument. But, it is not worth our while to argue it to-day. We know that large sums have been invested in this industry. We know that large iron industries exist in the country, and while we may not approve of the policy under which they are established, we have no desire to see them snuffed out now. As in dealing with all other countries, we have shown a very large measure of consideration, so we desire to show fair consideration to the iron industry. Therefore, we say, if it is in the
interests of the people of Canada that there shall be a reduction in the duty on iron we are ^ prepared to accept the responsibility of advising that the bounties on iron should be increased for a term of years in order that this industry may 'have a fair chance for existence	 Now we are willing to pay a bounty on iron 'manufactured in Canada for consumption in Canada, but we have no idea of paying the manufacturers of pig iron or other iron a bounty to enable them to supply the world with cheap iron. Therefore, we say that the bounty shall be applied to iron produced in 'Canada for consumption In the Dominion, and if this iron is shipped beyond the Dominion we have the right to impose an export duty upon .it equal to the bounty paid by the government of Canada.
I may say in passing, that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance withdrew that portion of his resolution before it was adopted, so that, in the end, it passed this House as a bounty on iron, with no exclusion of iron which should be exported after having received the encouragement of that bounty. Now, as further indicating the importance of the industry in the eyes of the Finance Minister, let me quote the very apt language which he used with regard to It when he introduced the system of bounties in 1899. I lay stress upon this because it indicates that the government as well as the opposition are alive to the necessity of maintaining and continuously developing in Canada an industry possessing so great importance ns that to which this motion of mine is directed. Speaking on the 13th .tune, 1899, the hon. Minister of Finance said, as' reported in ' Hansard,' page 4,973
Cape Breton possesses advantages of a very marked character for the iron and steel business. The great things required in this business -are large bodies of ore, large bodies of coal, large bodies of limestone and large capital. It is only by having these in combination that you can make a successful iron industry. There is a very large deposit of iron In Cape Breton, hut, apart from that, this gentleman has obtained an option upon and is now virtually in control of a very valuable iron property In the sister colony of Newfoundland, the ore from which is found ito blend very well with the native ore, while the Nova Scotia coal is admirably adapted for the work of smelting. Consequently, with the iron ore of Cape Breton available and the ore of Newfoundland so near that it can be brought to the coal at a very small cost, with large capital and with limestone in profusion, all the elements required for the successful carrying on of the iron industry are combined in that locality, and I have no doubt that if that gentleman and his associates take hold of the matter, they will carry on the business on a large scale. Nor does it end there ; for we all know that the establishment of a successful iron business means the establishment of other businesses that grow out of it.
And In dealing with that question, my hon. friend, the Minister of Finance, after referring to the great shipbuilding industry which years ago was developed in the province of Nova Scotia and the other maritime provinces, went on to say :

Not having an iron industry, the business of shipbuilding has passed away from us with the passing of the wooden ship.
Then further on he remarks :
With the improvements that are going on. the deepening of our canals, the opening of the Rainy River railway, and other things that are being done to improve the transportation of the products of Canada, there will be a large development of the iron industry on the great lakes and also upon the coast ; and out of this,
I strongly hope we shall see a revival of that shipbuilding industry which was so important in Nova Scotia, New Brunswick and Prince Edward Island in by-gone years, the revival of which would have such great effect in promoting the prosperity of our country. This has been happily described in Canada's growing time. Such, I believe, it will prove to be with regard to this industry.	*
And again :
I believe that the time is more auspicious for the development of an iron and steel industry than for years past, and I hope that with the announcement of this policy-a policy of certainty, because we give certain encouragements for a few years to come-we shall see a large expansion of this important iron and steel industry and that through it much will he done for the advancement of the welfare of the people of Canada.
Such, Mr. Speaker, was the attitude of this government with regard to this industry in the year 1897, and again in 1899. I am quoting from the financial exponent of the government's policy for the purpose of showing that the government, then at least, was alive to the necessity of giving adequate protection to this important industry, and was also fully seized of the fact that Canada, for an industry of this kind, possessed advantages and resources such as are possessed by few other countries in the world.
Now, Mr. Speaker, let us examine for a moment the progress of the iron and steel industry in other countries during the past few years. It is an industry, as I have already said, which was protected in Great Britain for a large number of years, and I want to point out to the House the growth of that industry in Great Britain as compared with its growth in Germany and the United States, both of which latter countries have protected it by a heavy tariff. I want to compare the growth of these three countries during the past twenty years, to show what has been done by those two latter countries under a protective tariff, to develop and increase an industry which is of such vital importance to every country in the world possessing the raw material and resources thereof :

That has been done under a protective tariff, and that has been done in face of the iron and steel industry of Great Britain, which in 1883 led the world, and in which the British economists of that day thought Great Britain would still continue to lead the world for all time to come.
Now, I submit these figures, Mr. Speaker, for the purpose of showing two things : in the first place, that you cannot find, so far as I am aware, anjT country in the world where the iron and steel industry has not required protection of some sort in the first instance to give it a firm ground and to show in the next place, by the example of the United States and of Germany, that if you have a country which does possess the raw material and resources which are required for building up an industry of this kind, you can, by giving the proper protection to that industry, develop it to an extent that would hardly be dreamed of unless you had the actual results before you which I have presented to the House.
Now in Canada at the present time, we possess, as I have said, every material in abundance that is required for the purpose of developing this industry. We use in Canada a very considerable amount of iron, and we shall use in Canada for years to come a great deal more, as our system of railways develops, and as our industrial development increases. We know that for the purpose of railways, iron and steel are used very largely, we know that for the purpose of building, for the purpose of manufacture, for the purpose of warehouses in cities, for all the purposes that are necessary in connection with the industrial life of our country, iron and steel are very important factors indeed, and we may well assume that the consumption of iron and steel in this country will increase more rapidly in the future," much more rapidly than our population itself is likely to increase.
Coming back for a moment to the United States of America, and referring to the

development of the industry there, let us bear in mind there are to-day employed in the iron and steel industry of that country more men than in any other single industry in the United States of America, that $122,710,193 was paid out in wages in this industry alone ; that the total value of the production in 1900 was $835,759,034 ; and that over one-third of this production was consumed in the construction of rails, cars, locomotives, bridges, buildings and electrical machinery.
I have prepared a table showing the imports into Canada of iron and steel for the year ending 30th June, 1902, and although I know it is a little wearisome to give these figures to the House, still, I will ask the House to bear with me while I give them, and after I have given them I will state the total result of the figures contained in the official returns. Now, Mr. Speaker, considering that we have the resources in Canada that I have mentioned, considering that we have some measure of protection in Canada and considering that the government provided a system of bounties in 1899, why is it that we find at the present time that the iron and steel industry of Canada is not in a very flourishing condition. I am not going into the history of any individual industry, nor do I propose to make any references thereto beyond this, that, looking around us at the condition of Canada we will all agree that the iron industry is not in that flourishing condition in which hon. gentlemen on both sides of this House, having at heart the best interests of this country, would desire to see it. What is the reason for this ? Well, the reason I think, in the first place, is the fact that we are side by side with a country like the United States of America, which jealously protects its home markets, which has magnificent resources for the protection of iron and steel and which has utilized these resources to the utmost, which now leads the world in iron and steel production and which controls the price of iron and steel throughout the world, because. I am told on what I regard as very good authority. that the output of iron in Germany today is controlled not in Germany, but in the United States of America. Well, under these conditions, what have we been doing for the iron industry of Canada ? In the first place, let me make a comparison : let me compare the protection which we accord to the iron industry in Canada with the protection which is accorded to the iron industry in the United States, and in the second place, let me compare the protection which is accorded to the iron industry in Canada to-day with the protection which was accorded to it under the Conservative tariff of 1894. You have the enormous country, the United States, to the south of us with all these resources I have referred to. you have that country with a home market of 75.000.009 or 80.000.000 of people and you have in that country the iron and steel industry protected by customs duties which are absurdly higher, I was going to say. than those with which we seek to protect the iron industry in Canada to-dav. Let us have no misunderstanding on this point. The right hon. leader of the government (Sir Wilfrid Laurier) claims to be a free trader and is glad, having begun his life as a protectionist, that he is now a free trader. I am not finding fault with that. The right hon. gentleman is. of course, at liberty to select his own policy but let us have an understanding upon this point. Are we to have a policy to protect and develop the iron industry or not ? Now. that is the question, which presents itself ' to this government and in proposing the

resolution which I shall submit to.the House in a moment, I am not going to propose a resolution which the government need necessarily take as a motion of want of confidence. X have carefully abstained from putting in the resolution one single word of censure or reflection upon the government, and in any comparisons I make in regard to duties, I want it to be distinctly understood that my sole object is to get protection for the iron industry of Canada, because I believe that protection is necessary in the interests of the people of Canada as a whole to-day.
In the first place, I want to make a comparison between the duties which are levied in the United States upon iron and steel products coming into that country and the duties which are levied upon similar products coming into this country and see how the comparison stands. Remember that the iron and steel industries of the United States have for their support a home market of 75,000,000 or 80,000,000 of people with greater industrial development than we can hope to have for years to come, and one would suppose if the iron and steel industry is to flourish at all in Canada that we must have protection approaching in some measure at least to that which has been found necessary in the United States for the purpose of building up that industry in that country. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) said years ago that if the iron industry could not succeed with the protection it had. it would be better to give up paying any attention to either iron or coal and devote our time to digging potatoes and other agricultural pursuits, but I do not think my hon. friend is of that opinion to-day. I have done him the credit of quoting his remarks in 1S97 and in 1899, which are in somewhat marked contrast, with the utterance to which I have just referred and which was made by him in the year 1887. and I trust that the Finance Minister has not departed from the view which he took in 1899 as well as in 1897 of the importance of the iron industry in Canada. And having that in mind ; and my right hon. friend the Prime Minister having that in mind-because the Minister of Finance spoke for the government with regard to this subject-let us see what measure of protection we have in this country as compared with that which has developed to so enormous an extent these great industries in the United States.
The United States' tariff, particularly the iron tariff is very complex, and is a very carefully thought out production, and it has not been easy in all cases to make an exact comparison between the Canadian tariff and the United States' tariff, but in some instances at least that comparison is possible, and I will point out to the House what the difference 1 si between the duties which are thought necessary even to-day in the ITnited States, and those which we grant as a mea- | Mr. BORDER (Halifax),
sure of protection to this great Canadian industry.

The House will see from this table, that in almost every item of the United States' tariff, certainly in every important item, the steel industry in the United States of America receives a measure of protection which is much larger than we give to that industry in Canada.
Now, I am aware that this government iu the year 1899 brought down certain resolutions for the purpose of giving support to the iron industry and causing it to be developed in this country, and I have already referred to the language of the Minister of Finance on that occasion when he dwelt upon the importance of this industry. Encouragement by way of bounty was given to the production of certain forms of iron in Canada for the reason that the tariff had been materially reduced in 1897, and it was announced upon that occasion by the Minister of Finance that the reason for extending the time for- the bounties was that it was desirable to give the iron industry a fair chance in Canada, and it could only receive that fair chance by obtaining some compensation for the reduction in duties which had been made in the tariff of 1897 as compared with that of 1894. But, I do not know Whether the House is really impressed with the very great reduction which was made in the tariff of 1897, and therefore I shall take the liberty of reading to the House some items in that tariff which show the serious reduction in the protection of this industry which was then effected.
And I may say in passing, that while the system of bounties may for the time being
give support to the iron and steel industry in this country or any other country ; I, for my own part, do not believe that the iron and steel industry in Canada can ever be put upon a solid basis, upon a permanent footing, unless we have something more than these bounties can give; unless we have actual protection in Canada such as will secure for our own producers our own market.

Is there any reason why we should not give in Canada adequate protection to the iron and steel industry ? If we give to it the protection which it should have, having regard to our raw materials, and the resources of our country, will it follow that there will be any permanent increase in prices in this country ? Well, Sir, let us look at the lessons of the past with regard to that. We have taken the duty from binder twine; we have to some extent taken the duty from coal oil; we have taken the duty altogether from barbed wire; and yet, every one of these articles commands a higher price in Canada to-day than it did at the time the Conservative tariff was in force. Let us look at the history of the United States. Thirty years ago in that country steel rails were quoted at 8112 a ton ; in 1902 they were quoted at $28; No. 1 foundry pig iron was quoted at $48 a ton, now it is quoted at $22.19 ; bar iron, rolled, was $97.63 per ton, now it is $47.79; cut nails have come down in price from $4.92 to $2.29; and so on, through the whole list of products of iron and steel in the United States. Can we not trust, Mr. Speaker, to the competition, the enterprise and the ability of our own business men to keep prices down in Canada ? Let us look around Canada to-day and see the industries which have flourished. Can any hon. gentleman on either side of the House tell me that, in respect of those industries which have had a fair and adequate measure of protection in Canada, any undue price has been exacted from the consumer ? I have paid some attention to this question; I have looked around for evidence upon it, and I do not Mr. BORDER (Halifax),
know of one single instance in Canada in which an industry has been developed by protection and the price to the consumer is not a fair price, brought down to a fair basis by the very competition which exists in the country among our own people. So I say I do not think we have anything to fear in Canada from giving an adequate measure of relief to this industry.
1 see no reason therefore why the government should not restore to that iron and steel industry the protection at least which it formerly enjoyed, and I should be inclined to think that in giving that question all the consideration and the attention it deserves, they might well take into consideration whether or not the protection wthich existed under the Conservative tariff of 1894 should not, so far as some of the articles are concerned, at least, be very materially increased, with every advantage to the true interests of the people of Canada as a whole. In giving the Canadian duties upon certain articles on which the duties are low' or which are free, I should have said that the duties I have mentioned are in some cases those imposed upon articles imported into Canada for the purposes of manufacturing. That is the case with regard to two or three of the articles I have mentioned, and I state this in order that my hon. friend the Minister of Finance or my right hon. friend who leads the House may not suppose that I am under any misapprehension with regard to the actual condition of the duties on the articles I have named.
I believe that it is the duty of this government to take this matter into consideration at once, if they, have not already done so. I would have been glad, had the government so desired, to let this motion stand over until a later day for that purpose but as no request of that kind was made me, I feel it my duty to proceed with my amendment. It is not made with any idea of staying the hand of the government or hampering the government, but with the profound conviction that it is necessary, in the interests of Canada to-day, in the interests of the iron industry, upon which the homes and fortunes of so many of our people depend, that we should have some greater measure of protection to that industry. I recognize the fact that in dealing with the duties upon iron and steel, the government would be obliged to give consideration to other industries in this country, and probably to revise our tariff in respect of many articles into the manufacture of which iron and steel enter. So far as we on this side are concerned, we are not afraid of that position. We believe that there should be a revision of the tariff generally, and if the government, in deciding to give some measure of Increased protection to the iron and steel industry, finds it necessary to make some revision of the tariff in connection with articles into the manufacture of which iron and

steel enter, we on this side will be glad to lend them a helping band and support them in that measure of protection to those' industries which we think the true interests of this country demand. So that considering the Importance of this industry, even if it should prolong this session to a greater extent than anticipated, even if it should involve a more complete revision of the tariff than might occur to one at first blush, I say that, having a regard to the condition of affairs in this* country at present, the parliament of Canada could do no better work than give attention to that revision at once. The homes of ten thousand or fifteen thousand people may depend on the action which the government will take. A very important industry in the province of Nova Scotia may come to a standstill, a very important industry in the west may have to cease operations. I question if hon. gentlemen in this House adequately realize what a blow it would be to the future of Canada, not only to the iron and steel industry, but to Canada as a whole, if these industries, in which so many millions of dollars have been invested in the past few years, should come to a standstill. No one can overestimate what it would mean to this country should that come to pass. No one can exaggerate what effect it might have upon general financial conditions, and I therefore say that if this amendment of mine, calling for increased protection to the iron and steel industry, should involve a somewhat general revision of the tariff, the parliament of Canada could not do better work this summer than devote its attention to that subject. I do not know that there is one hon. gentleman in this House who is not so seriously impressed with the present condition of affairs that he would be unwilling to sacrifice some of his time and comfort for the purpose of remaining here even longer than we anticipated, in order that a measure of protection, adequate to the needs of this industry and to the condition of the country, might be given. Therefore, not to detain the House at greater length, but in the sincere hope that the government may see fit to extend some measure of protection to this industry, and in the sincere hope that the government may be willing to accept this resolution as one urged from this side is in the best interests of the country, I beg to move :
That all the words alter the word " That " in the proposed motion be struck out and the following substituted therefor :
This House is of opinion that the tariff of customs duties should give such protection to iron and steel industries as will not only secure to our own producers and manufacturers the Canadian market in articles now produced or manufactured in this country, but will also develop and sustain the manufacture in Canada of other iron and steel products which at present are imported in large quantities from other countries.
And that the present tariff of customs duties should be now readjusted on ^his principle.

Among the many sins laid at the door of this government, I for the first time now hear the charge that we have been lacking in generosity and liberality to the iron industry. I have heard it said from time to time that we have dealt too liberally with that industry; 1 have heard comparisons to the effect: You have done thus for the iron industry, but you will not do it for some other. It is a new charge that we have been dealing ungenerously with the iron industry. I suggested that when these resolutions came up that would be the most opportune time for the discussion of tariff questions. My hon. friend has preferred to take a different course. He has preferred not to bring this question up in the ordinary way of tariff discussion, but to bring it forward as an amendment to Supply. He has preferred to bring it up in that form which is always taken in the moving of a vote of want of confidence. I congratulate the leader of the opposition on the moderate way in which he has placed this very important matter before the House, but still I consider that his motion is inopportune. I have been in a position to learn what is going on, not for the last few days, but for the last few weeks. I know that this question is of vital importance to the iron industry, and I know that the interests of this business to-day are in such a state that certainly further consideration will be required. The hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) has referred to the building up of the iron industry in the United States from almost nothing to its present gigantic proportions. He told us that it was only when the United States adopted a very high tariff that the iron trade was developed. I admit that, but I also wish him to admit that the iron industries when first established were established by the Atlantic seaboard under unnatural conditions, the high tariff did not save them, and there is nothing left to-day to mark the sites of these establishments but a few spots

of rust. It was only when the Iron industry of the United States moved west, where iron and coal and limestone were in close proximity, that this industry commenced to prosper, and Pittsburg and Alabama became the great centres of the United States iron industry of which such boast is made. This phase of the subject has not been considered by hon. gentleman in treating of this matter. The hon. gentleman from Pictou (Mr. Bell) also told us that it was under protection that the iron industry of Great Britain developed. I must contradict that. Last year when I had the honour to speak in the budget debate I quoted from a number of authorities to show that that 'business did not develop under protection ; that in fact the direst distress in the history of the British workman existed for several decades under the highest protection, and that it was not until the raw material of her trade, which does not consist alone in iron, lime and coal, but which consists largely of food and other raw materials ; it was not until these were made free and until the shipping of Great Britain was made free, that the great iron trade of that country developed.
Let me deal for a few moments with the iron development in Canada. I think hon. gentlemen, irrespective of politics, will agree with me that the growth of the Canadian iron industry has been slow and unsatisfactory, and has not yielded the results that were anticipated by the protection afforded in former years. Let me point out to hon. gentlemen that so unpopular was the history of the iron industry in Canada that in 1899, when the Minister of Finance brought down his bounty measure, the Hon. George E. Foster, whom we all know, was opposed to that measure, rose from his seat and walked out of the House.

I do not wish the hon. gentleman to misunderstand me, nor do I wish to cast any reproaches upon the management of that business. The Nova Scotia steel business was taken up by good practical men, who worked first in a small way, and developed their business; and all credit is due to them for the development which has taken place, not only tin their own business, but in the business of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. It was their knowledge, acquired under these adverse conditions, which made those men trusted by the investors in the iron business of this country.
Now, I think I have made my point. There are one or two other iron businesses in Canada, one in Quebec and one in Ontario, neither of which was at all prosperous under the high tariff of hon. gentlemen opposite. But my point is this : The development of the iron business in every country where it has been developed has been slow. Every iron business is a matter of slow growth,



and you cannot at all times ascribe the fact that an Iron business does not succeed to any relationships of tariff to that business. We have seen iron businesses developed under a low tariff; we have seeu iron businesses fail under a high tariff. In 1897, the gentlemen who established the Nova Scotia steel business, after having for several years tested in their own furnaces at New Glasgow, the possibility of manufacturing iron from Newfoundland ore and Cape Breton coal and limestone, came to the town of Sydney, and made a proposition to the town to grant them certain concessions. They came to the Nova Scotia legislature iu the winter of 1898, and obtained a charter. They came to the Dominion House later in the same year, and asked for the imposition of iron bounties. It was inopportune at that time for the ministry of the day to comply with their request; but in the following year my hon. friend the Minister of Finance brought down his scheme for encouraging the business by a system of bounties.
Now, I want to point out this to the House, that the gentlemen who promoted that industry, and who, we may suppose, looked deeply and broadly into the matter, and also looked ahead, ought to have known, when they asked for those bounties, that they would be effective to place that iron business on a sound footing.
It is one of the misfortunes of the case that evidently the bounties, did not entirely meet the requirements; but I wish' also to point out that when in 1897 the present tariff was 'brought down and the old tariff was revised, provision was made to assist or protect to some extent the established iron business of the country. The Dominion Iron and Steel Company, which is to-day the leading iron industry looking for assistance, was at that time unthought of. Protection was granted to the products of the Nova Scotia Steel Company; but provision was not made for such products as might be made by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Of course, the Dominion Iron and Steel Company might make the same products as those now made by the Nova Scotia Steel Company; but the market in Canada to-day is only large enough to absorb such lines as the Nova Scotia Steel Company Is now' producing; and if the Dominion Iron and Steel Company undertook to produce similar articles, there is no doubt that the two industries would be crowding each other, and perhaps pressing each other to the wall. We are afforded to-day, Mr. Speaker, the pitiable spectacle of a weak man, or a stubborn man -for both are in certain circumstances very much alike-when brought face to face with a position which he desires to avoid. Both act, in such a case, very much alike. How they squirm, how they hedge this way and the other, how they take a zig-zag, course, like a dog beating through a field, and then how they resort to every shift in order to postpone the evil moment when they will 135J
have to face the inevitable and do what they have always declined to perform. We have that spectacle to-day of the weak and the stubborn man, who knows in his own mind that the moment is fast approaching when he can no longer refrain from doing that against which he has protested for years. We are to-day face to face with a g^eat question :	Is our policy to be free trade
or protection ? For my part I have no hesitation in saying on which side I am ranged, and which side I believe the country favours and on which its prosperity is to be found. The ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was summarily dismissed from the cabinet because he advocated protection ; but if the cable despatches of to-day are correct, the hon. Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton) has just declared at a public meeting in England that the policy of Canada is moderate protection. Well, the last occasion, on Which I heard the hon. Minister of the Interior express his views, he was an out and out absolute free trader; and to my mind, the skip from absolute free trade to moderate protection is greater than the skip from moderate protection to adequate protection. If. therefore, the same measure of justice is to be dealt to the Minister of the Interior as was meted out to the ex-Minister of Public Works (Hon. Mr. Tarte), he should be summarily dismissed from the present cabinet. The bon. Minister of Finance says that this resolution is inopportune. But surely when this House opened, surely when the hon. gentleman delivered his budget speech, he should have declared what material alterations, if any, he proposed to make in the tariff customs of this country. He failed to do so, but apparently since then new light has dawned upon his mind: and if we are to judge by the statements of the hon. minister and those of the hon. gentleman who has just spoken (Mr. Kendall), there is a very strong possibility that the tariff on iron will be changed. If that be the case, then how is this amendment inopportune ? On this side we have for years contended that adequate protection was absolutely required for the successful carrying out of the Industries of this country. In that policy we have been opposed by the government, and it is only now. when disaster is apparently threatening some of the industries in the native province of the hon. Minister of Finance, that he finds himself compelled to give way to the irresistible logic of facts. Early In this year or at all events shortly after this House met, a wild speculation took place in the security of certain companies down in Nova Scotia. That speculation was based upon what the young men who went into it believed was absolutely reliable authority, that the members of the government bad promised the directors of those companies that they would largely increase the protection to the steel and iron industry.

I know not the truth of that; but I say that the members of the government ought not to be so uncertain as to their policy that they would allow speculators to bank upon the change of their policy. And, if that is their position, I say they are not looking after the interests of this country. Now, the fad of free trade is practically being thrown to one side. We hear very little about it. We hear it said even by free traders in England that the faddish free trade that is presented and upheld by the free trade school in England would not be acknowledged by Cobden and Bright if they were here to-day. It is the uncertainty of the government policy that is threatening us here with serious difficulties. My own belief is-strengthened by what I gather from the utterances of the hon. Finance Minister and the hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall)-that the government are still disputing and squabbling as to what their policy is to be. I do not believe that the government or the members of the government are united. I do not believe that they have made up their minds as to their policy. Had they done so, it would be their duty to announce it at once, not to lose a day or an hour. If they are going to alter the duties on iron and steel it is their duty to announce that policy at once. The alteration and readjustment of the duties on steel and iron, will, of necessity, mean the re-adjustment of the duties upon many, if not most, of the manufactured articles. And I was astonished beyond measure to hear the hon. gentleman who has just sat down proposing the theory that the tariff should be taken up and industries treated piecemeal. Could you imagine a more vicious state of affairs than the government taking one industry after another and saying : If you will support us at the polls we will deal with your industry and yours alone. No more vicious plan could be adopted. It would be absolutely impossible to have honest government if the fiscal policy of the government were carried on in that way, and I am astonished that any hon. member of this House should propose that any government should have power to deal with the tariff piecemeal.

speechtext:
If the sins of the present government were ghosts, we could stand them. They are not ghosts, but living realities. The government must face the question, and face it very shortly, whether they are going to swallow their whole policy. I would advise them to swallow it at once, because if they do not, they will bring disaster upon themselves-(I would not regret that so much)-and upon the whole country. Now, to show that we are getting into a condition that should make us a little anxious, let me refer to some articles in the ' New York Evening Post,' which I think, has the reputation of being one of the fairest papers in the United States. I have read it for many years, and I think that reputation is well deserved. In last Saturday's edition are to be found articles on the iron trade. One leading iron man, in reviewing the situation expresses very great uncertainty as to the reason why there should be a steady and continued fall in iron. This is what he says :-
The iron market is strong statistically and weak sentimentally. Statistics show that consumption is at a high point, and yet demand from buyers is very light. Prices have declined because buyers thought they would get lower prices-and they have.. Whether prices will go still lower or not is a question difficult to answer. They have at least reached a point where foreign importation is shut out, a factor which should tend materially to lessen supplies.
And another article, closes with this quotation -
On the other hand, the possibilities of the steel and Iron export trade, in case of a further restriction in home demand or fall in prices, is the most interesting problem of our industrial future. In the ten months ending April 30. our export of such manufactures was $19,393.000 less than in h similar period ending with April, 1901. An iron manufacturer was asked not long ago how he could afford to export any of his goods with home demand what it was

Now, here Is the key of the whole situation-
We are clinging on to the foreign market like grim death ; it is the spar which will float us when the boom collapses.
The foreign trade which he refers to is the export of iron into Canada to an enormous extent. That iron manufacture represents the iron manufactures of the United States, and he does not at all attempt to deny that they are looking to holding our market as one of the things that is going to save the iron industry of the United States from disaster. I believe it is quite possible that the Finance Minister is either wrestling with his colleagues or is being wrestled with, and the result may be at any time that we shall have an increase in our iron duties. It will come with very ill grace and, I believe it will come very unwillingly from the Finance Minister, because I believe he has some sort of idea that there [DOT] was a principle in free trade which he thinks

he ought to stick to. I think he does not regard it as good business, but, X believe he is a stubborn man and insists upon going a round about way to swallow himself or his principles. I would make this suggestion-that if he makes too long a circle to arrive at the point, he may arrive at it too late. I do not think there is any doubt about it that we have passed the supreme point in the period of our prosperity. It is so in the United States; it is so here, except for that one great outlet we have, the Northwest. If we have good crops there, it will carry the country through another year or two of prosperity despite the substantial blunders of the present ministers. But, if by any chance, we should have a failure of crops there we are face to face with a disaster in Canada that will appall most of us; for the manufacturing industries of the United States have attained such proportion that, with a fall of prices in irou of ten, twenty, or it might under certain conditions, of even twenty-five per cent in three months, we shall have, before we can remedy it, a flood of manufactured articles thrown into Canada that will practically ruin every Canadian manufacturer who is not, backed by large reserves of capital. Our manufacturers, during the last three or four years of great prosperity, have, 1 think, been very conservative, but they have still to expand, and the profits they have made have in most instances had to go into extended premises and new and modern machinery. If they should have a set back, they will not have, in most instances, the accumulated profits of the last few years to go on with; instead of that, they will have on their hands enlarged buildings, and they will have no use for the increased machinery, which will lie idle.
Now, I was greatly impressed when on my holidays during the winter time, to find what a change had come over Italy. That country, that we look upon as old and effete, is now one of the most thriving and industrious on the face of the earth. In Rome they are manufacturing in the most extensive manner. Ten or twelve years ago when the Grand Hotel was built in Rome, all its furniture, carpets and so forth were imported; to-day Rome is manufacturing its furniture for Canada, and you can buy it at Kay's, Toronto. The same with silks, the result altogether of very high protection, not imposed by the government, but imposed by individual cities to protect their own manufactures. That is an object lesson that we should take strongly to heart. I believe sincerely that unless the government face this question at once, during this session of parliament, we are going to have disaster in Canada that it will take ten years or more to get over.

It was not my intention to say a word in this debate, and I would
not have risen but for some observations that have just fallen from the lips of my hon. friend from Toronto (Mr. Osier). He desires to know what is the policy of the government upon this question and upon the tariff generally. I have to say to my hon. friend that his question is one which, at this time of day, it is rather late to ask, because the policy of the government was announced by my hon. friend the Minister of Finance a few weeks ago, when he declared that our policy was the tariff of 1S97. That tariff is a moderate tariff, which carries with it a good deal of incidental protection. That it is a tariff made for all time, nobody ever imagined. The conditions of the country change and vary. What may have been suited to our conditions in 1897, may not be suited to our conditions in 1904.
I will not particularize, I will take only the question which has been brought up this afternoon, brought up, as I repeat with my hon. friend, at a very inopportune moment The history of the iron and steel industry in this country has been a very checkered one. The hon, gentleman opened his remarks by quoting an article written as far back as 1885, to the effect that Canada is admirably situated to have and to develop an iron and steel industry. Everybody agrees with that. I remember that this same article was quoted, if not verbatim, it was quoted in substance, by Sir Charles Tupper when he introduced the iron duties in 188G or in 188S. Everybody who was in the House at that time will remember a certain celebrated and famous speech which Sir Charles Tupper delivered when he introduced a new tariff policy with regard to the iron and steel duties. His policy provided for still greater protection than had been supposed possible up to that moment, lie built great expectations upon it, expectations which unfortunately have not been realized. He expected that under the tariff which he was then promulgating we would develop a very large industry in iron and steel. But everybody is aware that the expectations of Sir Charles Tupper fell to the ground, that though the consumers of iron in Canada were saddled with heavy duties, the industry which he expected did not rise from the ground, as he led us to suppose. The gentlemen engaged in this industry struggled on, the tariff was amended from time to time, 'until at last it was taken up by my hon. friend in 1897. . Then he reduced it considerably, and adopted a more moderate tariff. Now, I call upon the hon. gentleman who has introduced this resolution.
I call upon the hon. member for Pictou (Mr Bell) also, to admit that the iron business never prospered, never developed and increased so rapidly as it has under the present tariff. The building industries using iron and steel, at no previous period in the history of Canada, have advanced so rapidly as since the year 1897. It is true that at this moment one of the great companies, is in trouble. But while that is so, every-

body must admit on the other hand that most every other industry in Canada is today doing a satisfactory business. We do not hear any complaints from them, we do not hear any complaints except from that one industry. I appeal to hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to admit that not only in the province of Nova Scotia but throughout Quebec and Ontario, all the industries using iron and steel are today more prosperous than they have ever been before. I do not think my statement can be successfully challenged.
But, Sir, let us come at once to the question before the House. There has been a good deal of excitement about it during the last few days. A great company which had been started with a great flourish, and which was supposed to be doing a good business, has, I am sorry to say, been the object of a good deal of stock speculation, and that great company has practically admitted that it was not in good financial condition. And if the whole truth must be told-and this is the secret of the speech of my hon. friend from Cape Breton, a secret however which is well known-that company has come to us recently asking for an increase in the tariff. Well, Sir, whilst for my part I have never hesitated to say that I am a free trader by conviction, and whilst at the same time I have favoured a tariff policy such as we have at the present time, that is to say a tariff for revenue purposes, carrying with it a good deal of incidental protection, at the same time I am not dogmatic, I am not a doctrinaire, and the government is not a government of doctrinaires. We are always ready to listen to complaints when they are made to us. When an industry, no matter what it may be, comes to us to make representations, we are bound to listen to them; we are bound to hear their complaints, we are bound to give a sympathetic ear to all who come to us with grievances, If grievances they are. But when a company comes to us in this way we have a right to expect that it will show a statement of its affairs, and not only so, but to show wherein the conditions under which they are working are unfavourable, to show why it is that they have come to grief, and why the expectations they entertained have not been realized.
When this industry was before parliament in 1899, and when my hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) introduced the bounty system which was accepted on both sides of the House unanimously as far as voting went, and with very little exception as far as speaking went, it was expected that that industry would be able to produce iron at $6 a ton. Instead of producing iron at $6 a ton they produced it at a very much increased figure. We have a right to know from them how it is that their expectations have not been fulfilled, and how it is that the prospects which [DOT]they gave out to the public came not to be Sir WILFRID LAURIER.
realized. We have the right to know also how their position can be remedied by a change in the tariff. We have a right to know whether or not the cause of their disasters, the cause which has brought them to the position in which they are now is really the tariff or some other cause. Therefore, under such circumstances, is it not the part of statesmanship, is it not the part which the government should take before we accept any other policy to see where we are and whether we can improve this condition of things or not or whether it can be remedied at all ? Within four days we have had these representations made to us, and if I do not betray any secrets I would not surprise any body by saying that we asked the gentleman who came to us to give us a statement in black and white which we could look into and study before we made up our minds whether or not we are to make any changes in our fiscal policy or allow it to remain as it is. That is the condition* in which we are at the present time ; yet, we are asked by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House to rush into a change in the tariff and come down with a different policy. I say that before we can come to any such conclusion we must look into the question. It is a time not for action, as stated by the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell), but for consideration, reflection and study. That is the position we take. That is the duty which is imposed upon us, and it is the duty to which at the present time we are devoting ourselves. That is the reason why my hon. friend the Minister of Finance a moment ago said this motion comes at an inopportune time. You had better wait. It shall be the duty of the government by and by to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and when we go into Committee of Ways and Means it will be for us to state the position which we take before parliament and the country. In the meantime, as hon. gentlemen pretend not to be actuated by any desire to make political capital out of the question, it seems to me that the best thing they can do is to withdraw the motion so that we can look into the matter and come to a conclusion.

the statement. The right hon. gentleman has had months to inquire into that statement. That statement was not brought down this week or last week. It was brought down before the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) brought down his tariff, two months ago. It was considered then. Why was that statement not asked for before the tariff was brought down 7 Was not that statement inquired into by the government before the hon. Minister of Finance came down and declared that with the exception of binder twine and steel rails, the latter contingent on the manufacturers being able to supply the home market, there would be absolutely no changes in the tariff this year. Now, we have the right hon. gentleman telling the House that the iron industry has prospered more under the present tariff than it ever did in the history of Canada, and he called upon the hon. member for Pictou (Mr. Bell) and the hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) to assent to what he stated. Well now, if that be true, if the right hon. gentleman is convinced of that, he will surely not assent to any tariff changes. He believes that is the best that can be done. If the right hon. gentleman is like the hon. gentleman beside him, and is willing to follow the hon. Minister of Finance, right or wrong, rather than follow the hon. leader of the opposition, he will no doubt agree with the statement of that hon. gentleman, that a protective tariff has never up to this period had anything to do in affecting the iron industry one way or the other in Canada. I can scarcely refer to a speech made by the right hon. gentleman during his tour through Canada in 1895, in which he did not call public attention to the iron duties in Canada and in which he did not state that these duties should be lowered if iron were not made altogether free. The right hon. gentleman pointed out that iron entered into nearly every industry in Canada, and he estimated that the burden placed on nearly every other industry was about GO per cent. When these hon. gentlemen came in, to satisfy the false sentiment which they had been teaching throughout the country, they made a reduction in the iron duties. What has followed 7 I shall not repeat the unanswerable statement made to the House this afternoon by the hon. leader of the opposition. He pointed out in the clearest possible terms, not in a general sense, but in the most specialized sense, the injury that has been done to the iron industry and the vast increase that has taken place in the importation of iron goods that might be manufactured in Canada in consequence of the policy of the hon. gentlemen opposite. I would like to ask the right hon. leader of the government and the hon. Minister of Finance if, after careful consideration when that statement is brought down, the government will be prepared to say that they made a blunder in 1897, and that they will
reverse their whole policy in making a reduction in the iron duties. I would ask hon. gentlemen opposite if they are prepared to be convinced by any statement that will be submitted by the iron industry that they made a mistake in 1897 ? I think this whole country is thoroughly convinced that it was a mistake. It is only a question now whether hon. gentlemen are agreed that they should retrace their steps and admit that they did make a very great mistake. Let us take the position of the right hon. gentleman's followers in this House. Let us take the time when these iron duties were reduced, and when the hon. Minister of Finance introduced his budget. Where do you hear the thunders of applause and the speeches that were made by hon. gentlemen on the other side of the House on that occasion ? I do not want to be offensive, but I say that hon. gentlemen were absolutely insolent in what they believed to be their strength at that time. They pounded upon their desks at every sentence that was uttered by the hon. Minister of Finance in connection with the reduction of duties at that time and now these hon. gentlemen are pleading for time. Never in the history of the House of Commons of Canada was there witnessed such a spectacle as to-day. The leader of the opposition, with great strength, with great courtesy, with great patriotism, with that clearness and effectiveness which belongs to him more than to any other member in this House, stated his case and gave ample evidence that his was not a motion of want of confidence, and the hon. Minister of Finance got up in a peevish mood and declared that the rules of courtesy had not been observed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the House rose at six o'clock I was pointing out that the position taken by hon. gentlemen opposite on the revision of the tariff has resulted in a succession of blunders. The first thing the Finance Minister thought it his duty to do was to shift the burden of taxation from foreigners to our own people. The iron industry, from its very inception in Canada, was protected by customs duties -duties which were very high from the year 1878, and which were never lowered until the hon. gentlemen took power. Up to 1897 the bounty on pig iron and on steel manufactured from pig iron was $2 a ton, and in that year it was increased to $3 a ton ; but, as was pointed out by the hon. leader of the opposition this afternoon, the Minister of Finance, in tones of considerable apology, and the Minister of Customs on the same occasion, declared to the House that the iron and steel bounties were given to compensate the manufacturers for the loss of the protection which had been taken away.
Both sides of the House in 1897 were committed to giving the increased bounties. The Conservative party of Canada had offered what was thought to be a fair measure of protection. They recognized then, as they recognize now, that if that great industry is to be put on its feet in Canada, it must undergo the same process, encounter the same difficulties and have the same assistance, that it has had in all other countries wrhere it has been put on a sound footing. For that reason the Conservative party did assent to the additional bounties given on

that occasion. But, speaking for myself, I entirely dissent from the proposition to decrease the import duties on iron and correspondingly pay bounties out of the pockets of the people. As an illustration of the effect of this policy, I may state that during the six years, from 1891 to 1896. when the Conservative party were in power, $436,876 were paid out in bounties, whereas during the #ix years from 1897 to 1902, we have paid out in bounties $1,800,000.
Now, I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance what he thinks is to become of the iron industry in Canada after the bounties cease in 1905 ? The hon. gentleman was very distinct in liis declaration that the bounties given in 1897, and continued for five years longer on the sliding scale adopted in 1898, were for the purpose of repairing the losses the manufacturers would sustain by reason of the reduction of the duties. I ask him now, not in an offensive sense, how does he expect the iron industry to live after these iron bounties have ceased, and it has no longer the protection which the hon. gentleman took away in 1897 ? His only answer will be to restore the bounties again, as he prefers to adopt a policy under which these bounties will be paid out of the pockets of the people, instead of one under which the foreign manufacturer would pay the import duties in order to get into the markets of Canada. There can be absolutely no doubt as to who pays the bounties ; there can be no doubt that the cost of iron to the people of Canada has been increased to the extent of the bounties. But the weight of opinion is entirely on the side of the position that the foreign manufacturer, in order to get into Canada to compete with the Canadian manufacturer, must pay the duties. The hon. gentleman told us, in his very able speech on the budget a few weeks ago, that when we imposed additional duties we increased, if not proportionately, to a large extent, the cost of the goods to the Canadian consumers. That is his doctrine ; but the hon. leader of the opposition this afternoon challenged the hon. gentleman to point out one single case of any magnitude or importance in which the protective policy had been the means of permanently, or to a notable extent, increasing the price of an article to the consumer. The hon. gentleman was content to sit down, after that long speech of his of two or three minutes, declaring to the House and the country that this was an inopportune time to introduce a resolution of this kind, and without attempting in the slightest degree to gainsay what had been stated by the hon. leader oi the opposition on so important a question. We will take for granted that the hon. gentleman has changed his mind, and now finds himself face to face, not only with the public sentiment of the country, but with a policy that is threatening one of the greatest industries we have in Canada.
Now, the House must have been much amused at what the hon. gentleman's friends had to say. The hon. member for Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall), who was put up to defend an industry in his own province, said that the success of the iron industry was not in any degree due to protection, and that he himself did not consider protection necessary for it ; but, after all, he concluded his speech by declaring that he wanted protection for iron, but intimated that there should not be protection for anything else. He thought there should be a sort of piecemeal protection, as he called it, given to iron ; it should be given to one section and not to another, and he urged the government to adopt that policy. Well, I do not know whether the country will take it that the hon. member for Cape Breton speaks for the government, or whether the government is too weak to speak for itself. The country certainly expected some declaration from the Finance Minister to-day as to what the government intended to do ; but he sat down without giving the House any information whatever. The right hon. First Minister declared that they were going to inquire ; that they were waiting until they had statements from those who were asking for increased protection ; but he also sat down without declaring his policy. I would like to ask the hon. Minister of Finance, since he has had his dinner, what the policy of the government now is on that question ? I would like to ask him, in the event of the government being satisfied that their policy of 1897, of making a slashing reduction in the duties on iron goods, has been the means of affecting the iron industry of Canada, if it is the policy of the. government to remedy the wrong they then did ? I am not asking that in an offensive sense ; but the hon. gentleman will see that it is a reasonable question to ask.
