speechtext:
The intelligent newspaper readers will have some difficulty in finding out just what the hon. gentleman means. He has told the House that parties who waited on the government had no fault to find with its policy. If that be the case the policy of the government must remain as it was in 1897. What are the business men of this country going to understand by the hon. gentleman's admission that the government have been approached for certain changes. What are these changes? They must be changes in the tariff. If so, these changes must be asked because the tariff of 1897 was a faulty tariff, for I defy that hon. gentleman to point out one condition now that did not exist in 1897. What was the condition in 1897 ? It was that we were largely at the mercy of foreign manufacturers. That is the condition to-day. Yet the hon. gentleman repeats again and again that those who are asking for tariff changes say that they have no fault to find with the tariff policy of the government. This is surely trifling with the intelligence of the people. It is time that the country should Hon. Mr. FIELDING.
be relieved from suspense. The country is titled to know what tariff changes are asked and what are contemplated, and what are the conditions which, according to the Finance Minister, induced those parties to approach the government. This is not a private matter which should be kept secret. It is a matter affecting public interest and concerning which the public should be given the fullest information. We were to^l by the Rt. Hon. First Minister that these parties who came to the government for changes in the tariff were the sole cause of their own difficulties, and that the government would require from them a reliable statement in order to verify whether the complaints they had made had any foundation or fact before the government would take any action. Well, Mr. Speaker, what we on this side contend-and we care not what the men who went to the Finance Minister for relief may have said regarding the policy of the government-is that the policy of the government is bad. We say that it is a mistaken policy, and we have that fact demonstrated to-day. Take the position of the two parties on this question. Do hon. gentlemen opposite believe that the iron industry has any future in this country ? If they do, they must change their policy. Is the hon. Minister of Finance going to come down with a proposition to give bounties instead of protection. If he is, I am afraid that the people will not at all agree with him. Are the facilities wanting to make the iron industry a success in Canada ? I do not think they are. My hon. friend the leader of the opposition pointed out clearly that we have every facility for producing iron in competition with the most enlightened methods in the world. All we require is the chance. All we require is a tariff which will give us our home market. If the government want to have the iron industry succeed, as we believe it will, if properly fostered, they must not face this question with a faint heart. The whole question must be grappled with. Contrast the positions of the two parties. The one party is shuffling in uncertainty, Its leaders are afraid to proclaim its policy, although they have a majority of some fifty at their back. They declare that their policy of 1897 and their tariff of 1897 are sound, yet we have them to-day in the humiliating position of being afraid to proclaim that policy to the country. Compare the attitude of the hon. Finance Minister and the right hon. the First Minister with that taken by the hon. the leader of the opposition. The leader of the opposition boldly declares his policy and takes the consequences. He does not wait to follow public opinion but takes the lead and creates a healthy, sound public opinion. A comprehensive, broad and courageous policy has been enunciated this afternoon by the leader of the opposition. He is not afraid to take the responsibility of his doctrines in this House and before this country. But the Minister of Finance

tills afternoon proclaimed the cabinet to be a collection of weaklings and its supporters a lot of mutes. There never was a more humiliating spectacle in the House of Commons in all its history than we witnessed this afternoon on the government benches. This iron industry is too important, there is too much money involved in it, there is too much of the future of Canada dependent on it, for it to be treated in this shuffling, uncertain, faint-hearted manner. We must have a defensive policy in Canada. Who would put his money into the iron industry with its present prospects ? with the tariff reduced nearly one-half, and in some cases three-fourths what it formerly was, and with this uncertain and unsound policy of giving bounties. Bounties can only be justified when high protection ceases to give the encouragement to manufacturing industries to which they are entitled. What does the hon. gentleman offer the country if our iron industries are embarrassed in any sense ? Has he invited men of capital to come to the country and put their money into it ? They will never put a dollar into the industry until the hon. gentleman changes his policy. No payments of bounty, paid out in dribbles and drabbles, and taken out of the pockets of the people, will give a home market to our farmers. Our people have to compete with foreign goods-I do not say in prices, for we are always able to compete in prices. But what the manufacturers and the farmers and all classes of producers in this country desire is that we shall have the home market which is the best market. What they want is the field, not the prices. The hon. gentleman knows perfectly well that we live in an age when a business must depend upon the amount of trade done rather than upon the margin of profit on each transaction. Now, I do not Wish to detain the House any longer. I have only to say that, of all the resolutions proposed in this House in the short time during which I have had the honour of a seat here, I know of none more far-reaching, more comprehensive or clearer in its statement of the case than this. Not only does it state the case with clearness, but it shows that the Conservative party are prepared to face the people with a policy that grapples with this Whole question from the raising of the ore from the mines to the manufacture] of the smallest article required by the people. That is what it means, and I know of no resolution proposed in this House that I support with greater pleasure or greater confidence than I do the one now in our hands.

speakeroldname: Mr. ROBERT A. PRINGLE (Cornwall and Stormont).
subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this is a great question, a question affecting great Canadian industries, and I hope in the few remarks I shall make, to speak upon broad Canadian principles. The hon. Minister of Finance, in opening his remarks, referred
to the resolution brought down by the leader of the opposition, and said that this was a most inopportune time to bring down such a resolution. But has not the hon. gentleman had ample opportunity to consider the advisability of protecting this and other great Canadian industries ? AVe find that, on the lOthi of March, the government met a committee of the Canadian Manufacturers' Association for the purpose of discussing with them the advisability of a general revision of the tariff. We find, Sir, that that committee reported to the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, and that, subsequently, on the 19th of March, they presented a tariff memorial. I am sure the House will pardon me if I refer to some of the things contained in this memorial. They say :
In pursuance of the interview granted on the 10th instant to a special committee appointed by the Canadian Manufacturers' Association, when they had the honour to consult with you relating to a general revision of the Canadian tariff, we beg to place before you a brief review of the circumstances from the standpoint of our association.
And they go on :
For some time past we have urged that, in the interests of Canada, her tariff question should he removed entirely from politics, and be viewed as a national business problem. As time passes and the tariff wars of nations multiply, we are more than ever convinced that in this we are correct; and we believe it to he the duty of the government of the day, irrespective of any party watchwords or traditions, to immediately adopt that policy which will best defend the Interests of our citizens and not only secure for Canada the development of her vast resources, but reserve and foster within o.ur borders those great industries which provide Industrial opportunities for her people. In recommending immediate and general revision of the tariff this is our sole purpose, and we believe we need no other.
Then, in this memorial, they go on to point out the great increase in the importation of the manufactured goods from the United States of America and the great increase in importation under the British preference. They also show the reasons why it was necessary for the government to take into immediate consideration the general revision of the tariff. They say :
Many of our industries have been comparatively prosperous during recent years. This has been due largely to the abnormal prosperity which the world at large has enjoyed, the partial protection afforded toy the present tariff, the growing excellence of the products of Canadian factories, and specially to the fact that the demands of the United States market, where industries are encouraged have taxed the output of the United States manufacturers to its fullest capacity. This home demand has been so great that recognizing the importance of their own market they have sacrificed their export trade, and speaking generally, have confined their attention largely to their own country. But even in spite of this, it is quite clear that any ground gained by the manufacturers of Canada has been only by persistent struggle

and that the price of the product will be steadily reduced. Now, he says further :
The courage of our iron and steel manufacturers in entering upon new enterprises of the greatest magnitude and the skill displayed by our engineers and mechanics in attaining important and 'Valuable metallurgical results must be a constant marve'l to every student of our industrial history.
The people who have gone Into this great enterprise in this country have had a good deal of pluck. They have had a good deal of nerve to invest their money in such a large and important industry, and I say that having done this it is the duty of this government to assist them in every legitimate way to bring that industry to a success. I- would like to refer for a moment to the great progress that has been made in other countries in this industry under a protective tariff. I do not intend to take up much time in that respect, but I would like to refer to Russia. We all know the experience that Russia has had under a low tariff, and we know the prosperity she is now enjoying under a protective tariff.
Ia Russia, in 1861. pig iron was imported free of duty and the free Import of all kinds of machinery and implements was granted, which, of course, operated against the Russian machinery building industry. It was not until 1880, however, that the privileges of free importation was abolished. In that year duties were levied upon all machines and tools made of *wrought and oast iron and steel. In 1882 the duty was made still higher. Under this Influence machine construction and the manufacture of rails developed rapidly. The railways now in operation began to bring ore and coal nearer to the mills, and. when the Ekaterlninsk railway in the south of Russia was finished, it opened up mines with inexhaustible veins of fuel. In 1884 the government raised the duty on cast iron and still protected coal mining. Almost yearly since that time to the tariff of 1891 duties have been levied to meet particular needs of the iron and steel industries.
The position we should take in this country should be identically the same as that which has been taken by Germany, France, Russia and the United States, and that is that duty should he levied to meet the particular needs of the iron and steel industry just as well as to meet the particular needs of all the other great industries of this country. When we consider the enormous importance of an industry of that kind to this country I say that it should receive every consideration. We know that in the manufacture of pig iron there is about ninety per cent of the cost which is labour. Is there anything better for us than that the labour of this country should be employed in the manufacture of iron and steel ? I do not think that I am stating it at all excessively when I say that the labour cost of one ton of iron is somewhere about ninety per cent. Some experts put it a little higher. The authority that I have referred to says that the cost of a ton Mr. PRINGLE.
of 2,240 pounds of pig iron, based upon a certain cost of material, is 90:8 per cent. In the same way it can be shown that over ninety per cent of the cost of a ton of steel rails, or any product of iron and steel, is labour. I have also the opinion of good authority, the Hon. Abraham S. Hewitt, based upon bis experience as a miner and manufacturer of iron. He said :
The value of every manufacture is made up entirely of the wages paid to produce it. Coal and iron in the mines cost nothing. They are the free gifts of God. But they are excavated by the pick and shovel of the workmen ; by him they are wheeled, carted, boarded to market ; by the workmen they are caried to mill ; by the workmen the furnace is heated and charged ; by him the iron is puddled, rolled, put up for the market, carried thither and sold. It is labour, labour, labour that constitutes every addition to the value of the article, and it is the man whio bestows that labour who should enjoy the fruits thereof.
I say, Sir, that the policy of this government ought to be toi protect the labour of this country which so largely enters into the manufacture of iron and steel.

subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext:
Let me point out that prior to a very high protective tariff being brought into force in the United States they had nothing but failures in that country. Men invested their capital and made brave attempts to develop the industry, but time and again they were crushed out by foreign manufactures. Up to the time they got very high protection, there was a constant series of failures amongst the very large iron industries. Mr. B. F. French in his history of the iron industry of the United States accounts for it in this way :
It is an established fact that in many departments of English industry, those who are interested trill carry them on at a loss for years, to aid in retaining markets from which they are in danger of being excluded by commercial restrictions or industrial competition; and scarcely a branch of industry has sprung up in the United States which has not, at first, had to encounter a severe struggle in con-seauemce of the foreign article being reduced in price below that with which it had been expected to compete.
But in spite of this handicap, the iron and steel industry in the United States has made remarkable progress since 1860. In every branch, as soon as an adequate duty was levied, the manufacture began and increased greatly while imports and prices decreased in an almost constant ratio. I have a list here of the failures prior to 1860, but it is sufficient for me to say that during that period there were a large number of failures in the United States. After they got an adequate protective tariff we heard of few failures of any moment. It was not until 1870, that the iron industry of the United States received adequate protection and really began to show what it could do. The production of iron in the

United States in 1867 amounted to 2,277 gross tons and in 1894 it amounted to L-017,096 tons which as you will see is au enormous increase. But I need refer more particularly to the increase from 1870, for the reason that in 1870 a very high protective tariff was placed on the iron industry of the United States. In 1870 the gross tons produced were 30,357, but in 1880 under a heavy protective tariff that production had increased to 864,353 and from that time down to the present day there has been a constant increase, except during the short period that the United States adopted a lower tariff when their productions diminished and when they were not as prosperous as when they re-adopted the high protective tariff. Let us see what protection did for the steel rail industry of the United States. In 1867 the importation of rails of all kinds into the United States amounted to 145,580 tons, and in 1878 it dropped down to nine tons.
An hou. MEMBER. What is that V

subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext:
Nine tons was the total importation of rails in 1878 into the United States. I will admit that some years subsequently the importation increased because there was an era of marvellous railroad construction, and the industry in the United States was not able to cope with the demand, so that in 1882, for instance, the importation ran up to 200,113 tons. But just so soon as railway construction slackened the importation of rails slackened also and in 1885 it only amounted to 2,189 tons, while in 1892 there were only imported into the United States 347 tons. The United States have been able to manufacture steel rails cheaper than any other country under the sun. They cut down the cost of steel rails some few years ago to $22 a ton, and they were able to underbid the manufacturers of Great Britain and Europe in that industry. That result was obtained under their system of high protection. We are familiar with the tariff history of the United States and we know that the Republican party in 1861 after a long period of low tariffs, inaugurated a high protective tariff and there has been an unbroken line of prosperity in that country ever since with the exception of the years between 1894 and 1897 when a low tariff was in force. Since 1860 the population of the United States has grown from 31,443,321 to 76,303,387 in 1890, an increase of 143 per cent. That was an enormous increase in a country which, if the argument of gentlemen opposite were true, should have retrograded under a system of high protection. In 1860, the national wealth of the United States was $16,159,616,000, or $514 for each individual, and in 1890. it was $94,300,000,000, or $1,235 for each individual. It is no wonder, Sir, that Gladstone made the remark that the United States of America, under her protective tariff, was passing
Great Britain, with her free trade policy, in a canter.
In the great manufacturing industries, the activity of the manufacturer and the earnings of the workmen show equally striking improvement. The cotton manufacturers have increased their consumption of domestic cotton from two and a half million bales in 1896, to over three and a half million bales in 1901 ; the number of iron furnaces in blast has increased from 159 in 1896, to 266 in 1901 ; and the manufacture of tin plates has grown from less than 40,000,000 pounds in 1894, to 678,000,000 in 1901. While I am on that subject, let me say a word in regard to that tin plate industry. We are all familiar with the attitude that was taken by the late President McKinley in regard to protecting the tin plate industry. The duties on tin plates and turned plates provided by the tariff of 1890 went into effect on July 1st, 1891. From that date until the close of the fiscal year ending June 30, 1897, the statistics of tin plates and turned plates were regularly collected for the Treasury Department. Let us see the increase under the protective tariff in that country. In 1892 the gross tons produced were 18,803 ; in 1901 the gross tons were 399,201, showing that under the protective tariff there was an enormous impetus to that industry.
Let us see what was done in the great industry of building locomotives in the United States. We know that it was not many year's ago when it was impossible for the United States to construct an American locomotive in competition with a foreign manufacturer. The foreign manufacturer chose to put his price down to the point where he could prevent the American manufacturer from making locomotives at a profit. But under that system of protection we find that American locomotives are running on American rails in every part of the world. You find them to-day passing the pyramids of Egypt ; you will find that the railroad now being built in the Orient, the Manchurian Railway, is being supplied entirely with American rails and American locomotives ; and, strangest of all, you find in free trade Great Britain that there is not an important railway on which there are not American locomotives used. That shows the progress which the United States has made in that industry.
But, Sir, I do not wish to be understood as saying that the only industries that prosper under a protective tariff are the great manufacturing industries. I recognize just as well as any one that the great agricultural interest is the important interest of this country ; and I could show by evidence that the great agricultural interests of the United States have prospered under protection just to the same extent that the great manufacturing industries have done. The Agriculture Department reports an increase of more than $350,000,000 in farm values,

and an enormous increase in all tlie products of the agriculturists of that country.
I have quoted from some of the speeches made by the hon. Minister of Finance. That hon. gentleman, like others on that side of the House, always leaves an open door. In a speech of his, made at a banquet in Halifax on December 12, 1902, the hon. gentleman was evidently looking forward to leaving an open door for some changes in the tariff. This is taken from the Toronto ' Globe's ' report:
If there is an inequality which needs to be rtmedied, we are prepared to consider it and remedy it. If there is a new' condition created by the establishment of some new industry ; if there are conditions abroad which are interfering with our trade ; in short, if anything has happened, we do not propose to shut our eyes to established facts, but we do say that whore the eo.untry has prospered under this tariff there is no reason for getting up an excitement for purposes of having us return to high duties.
Now, Sir, I say that something has happened. The manufacturers of this country, on the 10th of March and on the 19th of March, and persistently from that day to this, have informed the hon. gentleman that something was happening, and that the industries of this country desired that there should be a revision of the tariff. If the hon. the Minister of Finance meant what he said in the speech delivered on the 14th of December, 1902, he should, when he brought down the budget, have taken into consideration the revision of the tariff. I am not going into the figures of the importations of iron products .into this country. These have been brought out very fully and ably by the speakers who preceded me on this side. Suffice it to say that, according to the figures given here to-day, there are over $33,000,000 worth of iron products brought into this country, some of which are free, some subject to a very small duty, but the larger portion dutiable. Our aim should be not to encourage the foreigner, not to bring in foreign products, but to encourage our own people and our own manufacturers. No industry, such as our iron industry, with free imports or a very low protective tariff, can stand up against the huge corporation now doing business in the United States, and known as the United States Steel Corporation. That company is bound to control this market and will control it, to the ruin of our iron industry, unless the government comes down with an adequate measure of protection. We have had enough in this country of this * let alone ' policy. We want a government which will act and act in the interests of the Canadian people. The policy which hon. gentlemen opposite advocate is not the policy of the great statesmen of the neighbouring republic. It is not the policy of our late chieftain of the Conservative party, Sir John Macdonald, it is not the policy of the present opposition in this House. This is a matter which we should consider on broad Canadian lines.

subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext:
Are we to be told, as our manufacturers were told prior to 1878, that under no circumstances or conditions would the government raise a finger to protect or encourage the industries of this country, that if anybody went into any manufacturing enterprise, he did it at his peril and must take the consequences, and that it was not the intention of the government to interfere in any way to protect industry, under any circumstance. We have had the Minister of the Interior (Hon. Mr. Sifton), when speaking of the woollen industry, stating that if that industry could not survive under the tariff then in existence, it had better go down. I perhaps speak a little feelingly when I refer to the woollen industry, because I have the honour to represent a constituency in which there is a manufacturing town. In that town we had a prosperous, thriving, woollen industry, giving employment to from 150 to 200 men, but its doors had to close, and these men, who had no desire to leave Canada, had to go to the United States to find employment in the woollen industry there. But if the government had acted as it should, that industry, instead of being in crippled, would be to-day in a prosperous condition. We say that it is within the power and it is the duty of the government to give proper protection to the energies of the country, and to encourage and relieve distressed industries. That it can do by making such changes in the fiscal policy as may be necessary. Situated as we are, owners of the best half of the North American continent, possessing a territory stretching from ocean to ocean, with varied resources and capabilities, it is our mission to do everything that is necessary to make the Canadian people a great and powerful nation, and we should neglect no opportunity to lay the foundations broad and deep of future greatness. It is possible to do much by legislation. We are likely to have another great transcontinental line. I do not know whether it will be the policy of this government to subsidize that line or not, but if it should be the policy of this government to vote millions of dollars of the people's money toward the construction of that line, then it should be the policy of the government to see that these millions of dollars are expended in this country in so far as possible. As I said a moment ago, in my opinion the right hon. the Prime Minister should have gone further than he did. There are great interests to-day waiting the decision of the government. I think he should have announced to the people whether the government deemed it necessary to assist along proper lines the enterprise which is appealing to it for assistance to-day. I have no doubt that there are other industries which will make a similar appeal before the session is over. I would like to see these hon. gentlemen in favour of their own country. I would like to see them frame their policy

for the benefit of our own farmers, our own mechanics, our own miners, our own labouring men. Let them protect our own people. It is within their power to do so, but their policy seems to be to favour the foreigner and not the Canadian. I know that it is very hard for us, on questions of this kind, to separate ourselves from politics, but it seems to me that on a great Canadian question such as this we should be able to do so and consider it free from party prejudice. It seems to me that we should be able to come to its consideration in a true Canadian spirit, it is a question that soars far above and beyond party interest and consideration, and we should discuss it on broad Canadian principles. I have probably taken up a little more time than I had intended in speaking on the question of protecting this great Canadian industry. Ninety per cent of the cost of all iron products consists of labour, and there is no capital so important in this country as labour. I say that productive labour is the greatest thing we have in Canada. Its importance is incalculable. Just suppose that we have in this country 500,000 working men, whose wages averaged $400 a year. That is equal to the interest of $8,000 at five per cent, so that each labourer's capital is equal to $8,000 at interest. Multiply this by 500,000, the number of labourers, and it gives you capital to the enormous sum of $4,000,000,000, producing, at five per cent, $200,000,000 a year. That is the interest that we ought to protect in this country-the labour interest. This labour capital the Conservative party have always striven to uphold and maintain. It is, after all, the great national interest of the country, and it is this that we wish to defend against the ruinous effect of unrestricted competition. We on this side of the House have always been for cherishing Canadian labour, for giving it high wages, foy surrounding it with substantial comforts of life; and I say it should be the object of the legislatures of this country to protect in every way the labour interest of Canada. I know that my hon. friends on the government benches have many difficulties to contend with. They have these very clever and brainy gentlemen from the west who have settled upon a free trade policy in so far as they can. Let me say to these hon. gentlemen that they should take no narrow view of a matter of this kind, but that they should approach it upon broad national grounds. Let me say to them that if they take protection from the old provinces of- the Dominion, they rob us of that which not enriches them and leaves us poor indeed. Destroy protection in this country and you destroy the older provinces of the Dominion, and with the older provinces of the Dominion the great west would also suffer.
Sir, I hope the present let-alone policy of hon. gentlemen opposite will be abandoned and upon its ruin will arise a Canadian 136
policy protecting and cherishing Canadian industries, a policy which alone, I believe, will save this country. If hon. gentlemen will adopt that policy, I am satisfied that there will be no question about the prosperity and progress of the Dominion of Canada.

speakeroldname: Hon. J. ISRAEL TARTE (Montreal, St. Mary's).
subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am aware that a motion in amendment to the motion to go into Supply is usually considered as a motion of want of confidence. Under ordinary circumstances, the government are justified in calling upon their followers to reject and vote down such a motion. Has the government been justified, or are they justified in resorting to that procedure in this debate ? The leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) has very clearly and distinctly stated that he did not present his motion as a motion of want of confidence. It was rather, if I rightly interpret his words, an invitation to the government to relieve the present situation by making declarations proper to restore public confidence. My hon. friends on the treasury benches cannot ignore, cannot possibly ignore the fact that we are passing through an industrial crisis- it is out of the question. I do not believe that I am exaggerating the figures in stating that, during the last three or four months, there have been $100,000,000 of Canadian money lost. That is indeed a very large amount of money. I do not mean to convey the idea that the policy of the government is responsible for all that loss. All the same, the losses are there. And the last phase of the losses and of the crisis have come from the very industry that is under discussion to-day. For a time, the iron and steel industry was a very popular one. In my hearing, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister (Rt. Hon. Sir Wilfrid Laurier) said, a year or two ago, that he expected, before he was very much older, to see the Sydney iron industries rival the Pittsburg industries. My hon. friend must know to-day that he was then very far from the mark. The doors of the Sydney works are closed tonight, and my right hon. friend knows it better than I do, because he has information that is not available to ordinary members of parliament. Yet, I happen to know that I am not exaggerating, that I am not going beyond the mark, when I say that the doors of the Sydney works are more than half closed. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) whose good intentions I do not question, whose honesty of purpose I do not question in any way whatever, has said that he has one consolation after all, and that is that the opposition gave him the credit that the duties on iron have been lowered since 1896. That is indeed a poor consolation. What the opposition may think, what any of us may have said or thought years ago, is a poor consolation in place of



the loss by the disasters which face us today. And why are these losses so heavy ? Let me tell my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that it is because we have reduced the duties on iron. I am responsible for that reduction as much as my hon. friend is; politically I am responsible, although I am free to say that I have never had much confidence in the bounty system. My former colleagues will do me the justice to say that I have never had much faith in that system. The bounty system is not a policy, it is an expedient; and expedients have never led to any good results in the world. Capital cannot possibly have any confidence in a bounty system. If this country had gone firmly, energetically, into a protective policy on iron and other things, I make bold to say, we should not have had the crisis that we have had during the last month. And so much is this the case that to-day the men who are at the head of these large industries, are applying to the government to remedy the evil. If there was no remedy, they would not be here now. My hon. friend the Minister of Finance has told us, in his very short speech, that this amendment is inopportune. Why is it inopportune ? We have not been told. I would like to know what my hon. friends on the treasury benches have in their minds when they say the amendment is inopportune. Is it so because they believe that the opposition and men in politics who hold protectionist views have no right to place their views before the country in the way we are doing now. I know that governments do not like to see their hands forced; we must admit that governments are in office to rule. But governments are in office to listen also; and when my hon. friend the leader of the opposition said distinctly, that he meant simply to offer to the government the help of hon. gentlemen on his side of the House, it seems to me there is nothing inopportune in the motion.
Sow, Sir, the words of the Minister of Finance have been re-echoed by the right hon, gentleman who leads the House. He has told us that this is a time for reflection, for consideration, for study. My hon. friend has had a lot of time for reflection, for consideration and for study. For the last two or three years this question has been brought to his notice, the difficulties of the industrial situation have been made known to him as they have been made known to us. He knows that representations after representations have been made to the government. He knows that the iron men have come to us over and over again. He knows that his strongest political friends havei warned him. Let me quote only a few words from the Hon. Mr. Cox, who is a friend of the government. I am sure he will not be accused of being a traitor because he shares the views that other men hold, other men who are no more traitors than he is. In Hon. Mr. TARTE.
his speech at the annual meeting of the Bank of Commerce, in November, 1902, the Hon. Mr. Cox spoke these words :
Apparently thus far we are able to view with some satisfaction our position. But the tendency is clearly towards a condition demanding caution.
I shall not weary the House by reading the whole utterance of the Hon. Mr. Cox, who was then warning the country that we were in a difficult position. Mr. Cox knew then, what has been made very clear since. He is a financier who is at the head of several great banking and financial institutions, and he saw signs of trouble, he saw the signs of the times that we are face to face with now.
My hon. friends have been warned. During the last session of parliament, the Minister of Finance made a statement which is much like the one we have heard during this session. He inviited the country to wait. Not this session, said he, not now. The country waited, the manufacturing interest waited, the big institutions waited one year. That year passed away. At the opening of parliament this year the hon. the Minister of Finance invited us once more to wait. Last year the Loudon conference was to be held. It was a reasonable pretext. This year we were informed that the high commission might perhaps meSt again. That was also, to a certain extent, a reasonable pretext, but after all these are only pretexts. These arguments cannot inspire capital with confidence, they do not save us from the great crisis that hon. gentlemen have to take now into their consideration. We have waited two years, and we are invited to wait again. I know that it is rather late. The hundred millions! that are lost may not be reimbursed, may not be made up again, they are lost. Why should we wait any longer ? Sir, I do not wish to be a prophet of evil, but let my hon. friends on the Treasury benches permit me to say to them that unless they pause, unless they reflect a little more rapidly than they have done in the past, before we are much older we will have greater losses than the losses we are lamenting to-day. I make this statement to the right hon. gentleman and to his colleagues. They should know just what we know ourselves. They should know that great banking institutions are afraid of the present situation. I happen to live in a city where there are large institutions, I happen to meet business men, and I know what they think of the situation, and I know that my hon. friends on the Treasury benches have been made aware of the danger of the situation. Let me say that party politics should not interfere at a moment of crisis to vast interests. It should be no humiliation for the Minister of Finance and for his colleagues to come before parliament and to say:	Circumstances have

changed. The ministers are not infallible. If they would come before the House and say : Circumstances have changed, we are passing through a great crisis, let us change the tariff-they would be supported, not only by their own friends, but by their opponents. I know that there are in the rank and file of the Liberal party, not only In this! House but outside of it, thousands of men who think as I am speaking to-night. I know they would cheer my hon. friends on the Treasury benches, they would be glad if they would come before the House, before this session is over and say :	Well,
let us save the industries that are most in danger. I know it is late, the session is advanced. But my hon. friends, as I said before, have had time to reflect. I would not blame them one moment for what they have not done, if they would do to-day what they should do.
Now, Sir, my right hon. friend the Prime Minister said, and I believe there is a great deal of truth in it, that perhaps the management of the Sydney mines has not been what it should have been. Let that be so, that does not change the situation by any means. The fact that there may have been mismanagement does not prove that the Policy of the government is right. My hon. friends know it, and they know it so well that at the beginning of the session they tried to improve it a little by announcing that they would put up the duty on rails. What is true about i;ails is still| more true about dozens and dozens of articles of iron. I say it again, if there has been some mismanagement in the Sydney mines, that is no evidence that the policy of the government is right. Getting a statement from the gentlemen who are interested in the Sydney mines will not improve matters in any way. The proposal is an evidence of the unwilling' spirit with which the government is grappling with the situation-let me say it without meaning to give any offence.
The government should make up their minds that new conditions have arisen, that even in England, free trade England to which we are referred so often, there is a political revolution going on to-day. England was the only country in the world which professed free trade, and now the greatest English statesmen have made up their minds that long enough they have allowed other countries to slaughter their market, and they are right. Let me say it openly, I recognize the broad and statesmanlike spirit of the Hon. Mr. Chamberlain. We may not always agree with him in everything that he has done, but he has at least a pride in the great empire of which he is one of the servants. He knows, not only as a statesman but as a practical business man, that the industries of England are being) destroyed. He knows that the agriculture of England is being injured, and as a business man as well as a statesman he is not ashamed to say : Let by-136}
gones be by-gones. I have been a free trader, I have made free trade speeches ; now I want to protect and defend the industries of England against the unfair competition of foreign countries. That is a statesmanlike position. Why should my hon. friends be more proud than the hon. gentleman who is one of the' first statesmen of the empire to-day ? We may all have made mistakes. I am very much afraid we have all made mistakes, but I would not call it a mistake to have said ten or fifteen years ago that it was better to have a low tariff. I do not say that those who spoke in that way then are obliged to admit that they have made a mistake, but they must admit that circumstances have changed.
Sir, the iron industry needs' no defence. It is one of the most important industries that the country can see grow and prosper. That industry is intimately bound up with the shipbuilding industry. If the government allows, by false shame, that industry to go to the wall, it will be many years before it could recover. I would not hesitate one single minute if I were in the position in which the right hon. gentleman
is,	to take up that iron question and solve
it.	It would be solved very easily indeed. I do not mean to say that we could impose duties on every detail of the iron industry. There is a way of doing it. We know what we can manufacture. In 1897 we had scarcely any iron manufacturing industries. We were then only beginning. Our industry has been developing since, not very much, but it has been developing. We have erected great buildings for the manufacture of iron. We have plants to do that. Let us examine carefully and ascertain what these plants can make. Let us protect immediately all that these plants can manufacture. I would suggest to my hon. friends on the treasury benches, if they are good enough to accept a suggestion at my hands in the spirit in which I am offering it.vto raise the duties on a certain schedule of iron articles against all foreign nations, giving a preference to England. We would then import from England articles that we are not prepared to produce here. It would be a national policy, it would be a sound policy, and it would lead to a trade between this great colony and the mother country, and largely encourage our merchant marine while at the same time protecting our own industry. There is no difficulty in adopting this policy. The shares of the iron indus-tires are very low to-day. Would my hon. friends permit me to say that if they would adopt the policy I am suggesting this evening the shares would go up immediately. Confidence would be restored. I see smiling faces. I am not surprised, because I know a good many of my hon. friends in this parliament have lost a lot. But, outside of this Chamber men in perfect good faith have also lost money by leaps and

bounds. Let us not forget, as I said at tbe beginning of these remarks, that about one hundred millions of money have been lost.

Disaster invites disaster, and unless my hon. friends on the treasury benches make up their minds that they must grapple with the present situation, they will have to face more disasters than we have had to face yet. The great trouble to-day is lack of confidence. There is no confidence in banking institutions or in the industrial world, and X may very frankly tell my hon. friends on the treasury benches why this is so. Telling the country and telling parliament to wait until next year, to wait and see is not a policy. It is the lack of a policy. It is the absence of a policy. Capital cannot have confidence in such a state of affairs, and let me assure my hon. friends on the treasury benches that in what I say now I do not mean to impute any undue blame or give any offence to them. I mean to convey to them with all the earnestness that I can put into my words the conviction that I am speaking the truth, that I am making out the position as I know it is to be, that we are face to face with grave dangers and that in their own political interest they had better take up the question now than later on.
References have been made to the progress of the iron industry in the United States. The industry in that country encountered a great deal of trouble before it could take root. Why was it V It was because England was then a strongly protectionist country. Our English friends went very far. Parliament went so far as to pass an Act to prevent the emigration of mechanics or skilled workers to the United States. There was an Act of parliament passed in 1785 to prevent the emigration of mechanics or skilled workers in iron or steel or the exportation of any tool, engine or machine beyond the sea. Lord Brougham, in the House of Commons in England denounced the efforts that the young American nation was making to build up its industries. He suggested to the iron masters of England to undersell the infant American industries. In his speech, Lord Brougham said :
It was even worth while to incur loss upon the first exportation in order by the glut to stifle in the cradle these rising manufactures in the United States. '	[DOT]

An hon. friend behind me says * thanks.' It is the gentleman from the North-west that we hear so often speaking in such dignified language. My hon. friend from Cape Breton (Mr. Kendall) has urged the government to come to the rescue of the Sydney works. But he is a free trader. He has informed us that he is very sorry to have to come to that conclusion, but he came to it. Let me tell him that the Sydney works are not the only ones involved. The whole iron industry of Canada is involved, and all the iron men have asked the government for relief. We had a pretty big disaster at Sault Ste. Marie a few months ago. The crisis began there, it travelled down by the sea, and it is everywhere now. I believe that if my hon. friend (Mr. Kendall) and others who have influence with the government would combine with the independent members and with the opposition, we would carry the day. If we assure the government that it is the wish of parliament that those industries should be relieved, the government would come out all right. Let us tell the government that we do not mean to imply any want of confidence, and that is my intention in the speech-I am making now. One last word. The Prime Minister has asked: Why is it that the Sydney works have not produced iron as cheaply as the promoters of the industry thought they would That is a very pertinent question, and I think I can answer it. My humble opinion is that unless you give to an industry enough to produce, it is out of the question to expect cheap production. Quantity is essential in the cost of production. That is an elementary law. How can we expect that our infant industry at Sydney and elsewhere can compete successfully with the giants on the other side of the line, the giants of Germany, of England, and of France ? Let us start by doing the right thing. As the Minister of Finance said, the granting of bounties was a liberal thing to do. Yes; but it was not the right thing to do. A good many of us thought that bounties would help but that they would not be sufficient, because bounties will not secure the home market. A bounty means taking the

money out of the pockets of the people and paying it to the manufacturers, while protection, adequate duties, mean cheap production; it means the securing of the home market and it is because that cheap production has not been secured by sufficient duties and that enough protection has not been assured, that the cheapness that the Prime Minister expected has not been achieved.
In conclusion, let me say, that in my opinion the government would not only be justified but would be doing its duty towards this country by raising the duty on iron.
I know very well that other industries will apply, but it seems to be that fifteen days of consideration to a revision of the tariff could make it right. The government have a lot of material in their hands. When I left office they had it, and I have a very large amount of it myself. They have time still to consider it, and to come before this House with, if not a complete policy, at least a policy sufficient to relieve the present situation.

I feel quite at ease in expressing my opinion on this question, because I am not a convert to the idea of protection. Even when the hon. member (Hon. Mr. Tarte) was a member of the cabinet, and before he had decided to take his free course upon this question, I expressed clearly my opinion in this House that I was in favour of a bold policy of protection to the industries of Canada against undue competition from the United States. But because I am a protectionist, and for the very reason that I am a protectionist, I would not like to see this government or any government use what I have always considered to be the true national policy of Canada, as a means for helping stock gambling. Not that I say that stock gambling is the only question involved here, but I do say that it is deeply involved, and unfortunately it has not been treated of so far in this debate. Considering first the protection needed by the iron industry so far as it is covered by the motion, I wish to give the reason why I approve entirely of the position that has been taken this afternoon by the Prime Minister, when he said that it was impossible that the government could accept immediately the motion of the leader of the opposition. It is not my habit to attribute base motives to any member of this House, whether he sits on this side or on that. I am convinced that the motives of the leader of the [DOT]opposition are sincere and are patriotic, but we must consider the consequences of such a course as he invites us to take. The hon. smember for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has properly said that the policy of bounties "was a policy of expediency, that It had not the permanency of a policy of protection. And just because a policy of protection is of a permanent character, it would be foolish on the part of this government or this parliament to accede right away to the demands of the iron producers without considering what would be the effect of such protection on many other industries that are entitled to the care of this parliament just as much as is the industry at Sydney. Before the government grants any further protection to the iron and steel manufacturers, it is its duty to ascertain what would be the result of such protection to the farm implement manufacturer, to the manufacturer of carpenters' tools, to the nail and screw manufacturers, and In fact to every other industry in this country whose raw material is the product of the industry which we are asked to protect. If protection is to be given to the Dominion Iron and Steel Company-and I do not say that it should not be given-the government should be prepared at the same time to give an equally fair measure of protection to all those industries which have to buy their materials from that company or import them from abroad.
But, Sir, there are other industries than the iron and steel industries, and those which use iron and steel, that are entitled to the same care and attention of parliament ; and it would not be proper for this parliament and this government to come out now and say that because there has been a_ disaster in the stock gambling of this country, and certain industries are affected by stock gambling, other industries which are being conducted on a legitimate basis, and which offer to capital a prospect of a fair and honest profit, are not entitled to the same consideration at the hands of the government.
Therefore, the question that is raised tonight, with reference to only one industry, is in reality the whole question of the tariff. The hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) gave notice in the debate on the budget that he was going to bring into this House a resolution on the general tariff policy of the government. I could understand the hon. gentleman, on such an occasion, giving out the views he has expressed to-night-and I do not say that I do not partake somewhat of the views of the hon. gentleman ; I do not say that I shall not be prepared at some future time to consider the whole question of a tariff revision ; but whatever may be our different opinions of what the real interests of this country require, whatever may be the policy of the Liberal party, or the policy of the Conservative party, to-night is not the time, just because a few men who have lost money through stock gambling are coming here to ask for more protection, to raise the whole tariff question by a motion affecting the iron and steel industry alone.

As far as the first part of the hon. gentleman's statement is concerned, I am quite prepared to accept his explanation. But what I say is that the position put before us in the motion to-night is the position that has been raised by the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. It is the position taken by most of the newspapers, including the organ of the hon. member for St. Mary's. I do not blame the hon. member for St. Mary's, nor do I blame the hon. leader of the opposition, for the views these hon. gentlemen entertain. But I say that the government are justified in refusing to adopt such a resolution to-night. I say that they would not be entitled to the confidence of this parliament and this country if they would not withstand such a demand in a moment of excitement, because there are some men who, in good faith, and some who in bad faith, are now in a position to accept a motion which would mean an entire revolution in the fiscal policy of this country.
I will come later on to the question of stock gambling ; but when the hon. leader of the opposition interrupted me, I was just going to say that we are told to-night that the only remedy required by this large industry in order to prosper is an increase in the duties. We have been told of the great development of the iron and steel industry in the United States on account of a high tariff; but I would like, before this debate is over, to have an explanation of the statement that was made this afternoon by the hon. member for Toronto (Mr. Osier) that one of the dangers that threaten our industry was the state of depression of the iron and steel industry in the United States -the industry which, according to other members of the opposition has been so greatly flourishing under a high protective policy. Is the tariff in the United States lower to-day than it was five years ago ? If the tariff does not protect the iron and steel industry in that country, - born and brought up and kept under the most favourable circumstances with which any industry was ever favoured, with a huge monopoly extending not only over the entire territory Mr. BORDEN (Halifax).
of the American republic, but invading the neutral markets of this world, going to England and competing there with old iron industries, going to Egypt and supplying the railways there with American rails, going to China and superseding the English products there-I say that if such an industry is not prospering to-day, how can the logical conclusion be drawn from the motion of the hon. leader of the opposition, from the speech of the hon. member for St. Mary's, or from the speeches of the other supporters of this motion, that, by adopting the same policy, we shall avoid the disasters which the iron and steel industry of the United States has suffered ? I say that the conclusion is not logical that by adopting that same policy we would revive our industries.
Now, I am not going to enter into any technical details regarding this industry; I am not competent to do so. The hon. member for St. Mary's said that one of the reasons why iron cannot be produced at Sydney cheaply enough in the present situation is because the iron industry cannot expect a large enough market to develop and to prosper. But, Sir, the statement was given out some days ago by some of the directors of that company that it was not the iron part of the business that was suffering, but the steel production, and that if they were given some special protection on some of the articles of steel, the production would be revived. But the fact remains that under the present tariff, knowing exactly where they were, knowing what property they had, knowing what the population of Canada was, knowing the purchasing power of Canada, that company started some four years ago with a huge prospectus asking the people to subscribe millions and promising them large returns and profits, without conveying the slightest hint that the tariff was an impediment. Therefore, I say that my right hon. friend the Prime Minister was right when he said that the public of this country were asking for some explanation regarding the management of the Dominion Steel Company. The hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) has asked the government to declare immediately in favour of a high tariff upon most of the productions on iron and steel with a preference in favour of the British producer. I must say that I was astounded at this declaration, and it was mainly this declaration which brought me to my feet. It is well known that when the government decided to increase the preference to the British producer, I spoke of that policy with great caution. While I had supported' that policy in 1897, I expressed my fear that we were going too far in that line.

I am glad my hou. friend has given that explanation. 1 go further on that point, and that is one part of the motion of the hon. gentleman to which I wanted to refer, and I might as well do it now. I was just going to tell the hon. leader of the opposition that there iS| a part of his motion which needs some explanation. It is when he says that we should give- -
Such protection to the iron and steel industry as will not only secure to our own producers and manufacturers the Canadian market in articles now produced or manufactured in this country, but will also develop and sustain the manufacture in Canada of other iron and steel products which at present are imported in large quantities from other countries.
This is a broad statement. Does it mean that he would like the government to notv impose a duty on all iron and steel articles that come into this country, even those which are not manufactured and cannot be manufactured here with profit, because the market is not large enough, and thus impose on the other industries which have ' to use these articles a further amount of taxation without compensating them by other protection ? The hon. member for St. Mary's had evidently that position in view, when he spoke of the preference which we might give to British goods. But if we acknowledge that certain goods cannot be produced in this country, by what right should we prevent the manufacturers of Canada, who need those goods, from buying them where they can get them best and cheapest ? Why should we compel them to go and buy them in England ? In my view, Mr. Speaker, on these articles which we cannot produce, we should have absolute free trade. If by a certain amount of protection and without imposing too heavy a burden on other industries we can force the production of these articles in Canada, I am in favour of our doing so, because I am a protectionist; but since we cannot do that, we have no right to impose on those manufacturers the obligation to buy those goods in England. We should leave them free to buy them where they can get them of best quality or of best producing capacity, if machinery, and at the cheapest price.
I am just now coming to the point that I touched at the beginning of my remarks. The hon. member for Both well (Sir. Clancy) said this afternoon that the country wants more protection on iron and steel. The hon. member for St. Mary's division (Hon. Mr. Tarte) said that $100,000,000 had been lost to this country in the last three months by the policy of the government. The hou. leader of the opposition said that an increase of duty was imperatively necessary to save the parties interested in the manufacture of steel and iron. Well, as regards the loss of $100,000,000 within the last three months, at least nine-tenths of that loss is due to the fact that many people of the country lost their heads. If capital has become difficult, if bankers have become close-fisted, it is not because of the tariff policy, but because capital was forced into improper channels. The hon. gentleman has spoken of the opinion of the bankers. I know, as a matter of fact, that in December last, there was a consultation between the managers and directors of the most important banks of Canada, and what did they decide ? They decided, not that the tariff policy was wrong, but that an immense amount of capital was invested in stock gambling-for which they were in a large degree responsible-and they decided there and then to restrict supplies to stock gamblers. Certainly the decision was a wise one in itself, but perhaps it was hardly a wise decision, after they had enabled those people during nine and ten years to get money on a margin of 10 per cent, to close immediately their doors and bring about this slump in the markets.
The hon. member for St. Mary's has said that the bounty system is a policy of expediency in tariff matters. Let me say also on the part of many people who have money invested in the industries of this country, that black-mailing is also, for too many people, a good policy to be used in finance and tariff matters. The hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) says that for three years the government has been made aware of the situation of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company. Well, Mr. Speaker, the investing public was not made aware of it. On the contrary, the directors of that institution repeated time and again that the industry could not fail to be most prosperous ; and if these directors were going to the government for the last three years and asking for more protection, while at the same time they were enticing money from the people on the pretense that the company had a glowing future, I say that a thorough investigation should be held; and if the people have been robbed by the directors of the Dominion Steel Company, these directors should be held accountable before that industry is given any more protection.
What was the prime occupation of the company ? They issued bonds to the amount ol' nearly $8,000,000, at the rate of $85 for every bond of $100, and every purchase of a bond received in addition a paid up share of $100 common stock. So that the company gave a par value in bonds and shares of $200 for $85. They issued preferred stock to the amount of $5,000,000, they issued common stock to the amount of $20,000,000. they gave shares all over the country, and they made returns of the common shares to the amount of 80 per cent, because it was a tremendous industry and was going to be the best investment the people of Canada

could make. And during all this time, I am told by an ex-minister, they were going to the government and begging for more protection because otherwise they could not live. I say, if that is the case, first and before all, what the public of this country will demand is not so much protection for Mr. Cox and Mr. Ross, but that they should be made accountable for the declarations they have, made to the people of Canada.
Now, Sir, I quite admit with the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that the mismanagement of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company, and the way in which the people of this country have been led to take stock in that concern, is no reason for not having a bold policy on the industry itself. I quite admit that, and I am prepared to say now to the government that, after they have carefully considered the question, after they have taken into consideration the consequences that will arrive as affecting every other industry that is dependent upon this mother industry, if they are prepared to recommend an increase of duty, I do not say I will not support it, but I say

speechtext:
No, Sir. Before now I have asked the government for more protection than they were willing to give. My views on the tariff question are well known. I ran as a protectionist in 1896 and again in 1900 in a purely rural constituency where there could be no political advantage to me in advocating that policy. But I am convinced that, as the hon. member for Cornwall (Mr. Pringle) has said, the tariff policy of the country should not be made a tool either in the hands of financial speculators or in the hands of political speculators. I am in favour of a solid policy of protection for this country. That should be our national policy. But, because we make it our national policy, every part of it should be wisely considered, and it should not be changed on the spur of the moment because of some financial distress existing which arises from causes entirely foreign to the tariff. Let me add-I cannot give it as a piece of information, but as a rumour which has been current on the streets of Montreal for some weeks-that a high official in the Dominion Iron and Steel Company has thrown lately on the markets over one thousand shares of his own company's securities Perhaps that has had something to do with the fall in value of the shares of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company-perhaps nearly as much as the competition of the American industry. Therefore, I say, and I insist upon it, that, while public opinion in this country, or at least a certain part of It, may require that more protection should be given to that industry, what this country requires and immediately demands is that a thorough examination be made not only of the way Mr. BOURASSA.
the stock of the Dominion Iron and Steel Company was managed and put on the market and used by stock gamblers, but that the whole question of stock gambling should be considered by this parliament. Sir, if we wish to have confidence established for the capital of our country, if we wish to bring in foreign capital to support our industries, if we wish British and American and German capitalists to invest in Canada, we must make it known that no board of directors is allowed to speak one way in secret when they want favours from the government and another way to the public when they want the money of the public. We must make it known that when the public has been allured by false promises to invest in any industry, the government's hand is strong enough to force those who have made those promises to give an account of their deeds. We must make it known to foreign; capitalists thjat when money is placed in an industry in Canada it is placed in safe hands, and will not be subject to stock gambling on any change of opinion on the part of this director or that. We must make it known that no particular director has the right to give three times the value received without knowing that some day he will be obliged to pay back that capital and in the meantime to pay interest on it. I say that the hon. member for St. Mary's may be right when he says there should be a tariff revision. That is a question which should be studied. But I contend that I am right in saying that the time has come when this parliament should deal with the whole question of the stock exchange and the way in which strong industries in this country are placed at the mercy of speculators, of men who have no responsibility, who do not care for the future of the country or even for the general character or permanent stability of their industries, but simply care to raise money for the time being, whatever the consequence to the people of the country.

subtopic: COMPARISON OF RATES OF DUTY ON IRON AND STEEL.
speechtext:
In following this debate it has become difficult for me to understand whether the motion was intended to deal with a general principle or to apply to a specific case, whether it is intended for the purpose of bringing about a change in the conditions connected with the Dominion Iron and Steel Company or whether it was intended to deal with the iron industry as affecting the Dominion as a whole. I would like to deal with the question from the standpoint of its effect cn the general industries of the Dominion. Canada, situated as it is, and constituted as it is, needs iron as England needs bread. Cheap iron is as necessary to the development of this country as cheap bread is to the support of the industries of England. I believe in protection, but I do not understand the idea which seems to prevail with some of our friends that a mere increase of duty is protec-

tion, and that such an increase is a cure for every evil that can possibly affect the nation. We have had, in times past, a policy of protection to the iron industry. It was not a part of the National Policy. It was an addition which proved the unreasonableness of the high tariff policy and actually broke its back; it was the high protective duties in favour of the production of iron which caused our other manufactuiiug industries throughout Canada to languish in the latter years of the so called National Policy.
There is no part of the present tariff policy of the government which has been so effective in improving the condition of our manufacturing industries and improving the general conditions of this country as the reduction in iron duties which is part of the tariff of 1897. The iron duties were reduced in 1897, and the country benefited thereby. But it would seem as if our friends wished to create the impression that the iron duties were abolished at that time. I find on looking at the Tariff Act of 1897 that there are duties attached to the importation of iron and steel which seem to me to give a very substantial measure of protection, quite as much as any industry is entitled to under a revenue tariff. 1 find on looking at this list that pig iron has a protective duty of $2.50 a ton; that rolled iron or steel has a duty of $7 a ton; bar iron and steel 87 a ton; rolled iron and steel, in sheets or plates, $7 a ton; iron and steel rails, 30 per cent; fish plates, $8 a ton; cast iron pipes, $8 a ton, and so on through the list. Does any person suppose that the manufacturing and agricultural industries of this country can afford a higher rate of protection to the iron industry than is now accorded ? For my part I do not believe they can. Under any circumstances, and according to the knowledge which has come within my range, I am prepared to vote against any increase in the iron duties, beyond a mere readjustment thereof. I believe that in doing so I am acting in the best interest of the country as a whole. 1 find that not only is the iron industry protected to the extent I have mentioned, but that it is also bonused to the extent of $3 a ton on Iron and steel ingots, puddled bars and pig Iron. Now, I say an industry that is protected to this extent, and is further bonused to this extent, has certainly no right to come to this parliament and make a plea that it does not now enjoy a very considerable measure of protection and advantage at the hands of the country at large.
Now, a word in regard to the bonus policy and the difference between a bonus and a tariff. It has been said that the bonus is a policy of mere expediency. No doubt it is a policy of expediency or experiment, and why not ? Why should the country be committed without experiment to a policy the result of which no man can foresee,
or if he can foresee, it would be in the light of experience, and that would be that a policy of high tariff in favour of the production of iron would mean disaster to the country. I think it Is right and proper that if you desire to encourage iron production in this country-and who does not so desire?- the encouragement should be given by way of a bonus rather than by way of a tariff. Let me point out the difference between the cost to the country in the two cases. Supposing we produce 100,000 tons of iron in a year, we bonus that to the extent of $3 a ton, we pay a specific amount of $300,000. Supposing we put a protective duty of $3 a ton on iron and we import a million tons. It costs the consumers of that iron $3 a ton on a million tons, or $3,000,000 ; whereas the bonus only cost $3 a ton on 100,000 tons, and the iron industry of the country had just the same advantage on every ton actually produced. The policy of bounties is only a policy of expediency or experiment. But as one who desires to see the iron industry encouraged, and does not want to see the country itself or the industries therein wrecked, I have supported the policy of iron bounties, and am prepared to continue to do so to a moderate and reasonable extent in preference to an increase of duties.
In regard to the suggestion made by the hon. member for St. Mary's (Hon. Mr. Tarte) that if the iron duties were raised to-night, to-morrow the millions which have been lost, as the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa) said, in stock gambling, would be recovered. I ask this House if that is a proper reason to present to us. Does this parliament exist for the purpose of rigging the stock market ? Surely we have other duties to perform, other interests to guard than the interests of those who have invested their money under such circumstances. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that in the construction of railways necessary for the development of this country, in the expenditures on manufacturing industries necessary to keep pace with our agricultural development, we require cheap iron more than we do anything else. If Canada can produce that iron, and if any legislation can be brought forward or any assistance be given that will really induce the production of that iron by Canada as cheaply as it can otherwise be procured, then I am in favour of such legislation. But legislation which shall cause iron to be dear throughout the country, which shall cause an increase of its price one-third, or one-half, or possibly double-I say such a policy is not a policy of national protection, it is a policy of industrial and commercial suicide.
