I had not the pleasure of hearing what has been said on this question, yet it is of sufficient importance to excuse me for occupying a small portion of time. With the spirit of

the resolution I am in hearty sympathy. I believe it is in the interest of this country to protect the development of all its natural products. But the question arises whether the resolution itself, at this stage, is not of an academic nature, incapalble of doing any good, or of being made applicable in the slightest degree. If the resolution was propounded at the proper time, I would be glad to give it my sympathy and support. I believe in cultivating the iron and steel industry of this country, because I believe they are indigenous to it. I do not think that if this resolution was carried to-night the government are in a position to make it effective. It would involve a readjustment of the tariff from top to bottom. It would require an investigation into the manufacturing conditions of every industrial concern in this country that uses iron. It is a task that, at this late stage of the session, it would be impossible for the government to overtake, and it is not in the present instance an absolute necessity. Therefore, while I sympathize with the resolution, I do not sympathize with it under the present circumstances, because it is incapable of doing any good.
Now, it has been urged that a bounty differs from a duty. So it does to a certaiu extent, but in so far as any manufacturer is concerned it is exactly the same thing. It does not matter whether he is protected against the foreign producer by $G a ton duty or whether he receives a present from the government of $6 a ton. It does not matter if he is able to put his wares upon the market at $6 a ton less than the people who are competing against him. I take exception to some of the remarks made by the hon. gentleman who sits in front of me (Hon. Mr. Tarte) when he undertook to asperse the government and to hold it responsible for the loss of a large sum of money. The government is not to blame in the slightest degree,, because of the disaster which has overtaken some of the industries that may be affected by it. These people knew when they went into this business exactly what the tariff was. They thought they would be able to bring about a successful condition of affairs but they have not been able to bring about that condition. This disaster has not been brought about by the neglect of the government because it has taken no new attitude since the present tariff was inaugurated. My hon. friend who sits in front of me, says that over a hundred million of dollars have been lost by the people of this country. I think he is incorrect in that. I think the ownership of that hundred million of dollars has shifted. The people who had that hundred million of dollars a short time ago have not got it to-day, but somebody else has and in so far as the country is concerned, I do not think that any very serious loss has taken place. If we were to compare, as has been done here, the value Mr. HEYD.
of the stocks to-day with what it was in 1896, we would see that there has been an actual increase of several hundreds of millions, not of a hundred million, in value. The crisis that has been brought about and which has precipitated this discussion in the House is the result of an attempt to float upon an unsuspecting public manufacturing estimates that are not truthfully represented. Take the very industry whose condition has precipitated this discussion. We know that at the time it was floated the promises that were made. We know that the vice-president and manager made a speech in Toronto before the board of trade and we know what he said. I will read from his speech :
As to the Cape Breton district, situated on the seaboard, the whole wide world is her market, all of it, and In our modesty we do not ask for more.
At this point we must again revert to our cost comparison. Then he goes on to say in his speech that they can produce iron and steel at Sydney at $6 per ton at tide water cheaper than they can at Pittsburg.
I will be pardoned for a few more words cn the great promise of the Cape Breton district. So great is this promise that it has ceased to be local. It has ceased to be sectional. It has become International in its influence. To-day, Sydney is a familiar name to every steelmaker in England, and before another year rolls around the leaders in this industry will have beien with us to see for themselves the new centre. At this moment Sydney is debated with doubt and misgiving by the large German syndicates, and in the United States the strength of her position is conceded by every expert. Canada alone at this moment does not realize how splendid an opportunity is within her control.
That speech was made only two years ago before the Board of Trade of Toronto by the vice-president and manager of this very institution and yet we are told that the government Is responsible for this loss. These men have induced an unsuspecting public to pay three times as much for the stock as it was worth, they floated for about $28,000,000 a concern that never had more than one-third of that money invested in it. What can you expect ? There is not one manufacturing establishment to-day in Canada from one end of the country to the other, except, perhaps, those that are affected by the preferential tariff, for instance, the woollen mills, which are not successful and whose stock is not above par. I am willing to admit that the preferential tariff lias affected some of our industries, but I believe the surtax will do them good. I believe that in not more than a year from now' better conditions amongst the woollen and cotton mills will prevail. The iron industry w7as started a few years ago knowing the conditions which existed. The same conditions exist to-day as those which existed in 1897 and 1900. The government has done nothing to precipitate the disaster

which has overtaken this concern, and these establishments that have been over capitalized, and then floated upon an unsuspecting public must come to disaster. You cannot float a company and declare dividends on a capital of $30,000,000 when there is only $10,000,000 in the concern. You cannot declare dividends on water and keep it up for ever. To hold the government responsible for what has taken place is to make a foundationless charge. I sympathise with the resolution. I believe higher duties should be put upon iron and steel, but before passing a resolution like that to-night we must consider what it involves. It is simply an academic expression of opinion that it would be a good thing, but would it restore confidence V Not at all. It would demoralize all subsidiary trades and other great industrial institutions. If the industries which are engaged in buying iron were told that there would be an increase in the value of iron and there was a feeling of insecurity and uncertainty created in every large establishment that uses iron unless the government promised that it would make a corresponding increase in the duties which these establishments now enjoy. That would involve a re-arrangement of the tariff from beginning to end, months of labour and a great deal of study. We know that when tb,e old government existed and when the new government took office nearly a year was consumed in ascertaining exactly the conditions as they existed. It is as necessary to-day asl it was seven years ago to make careful inquiry and when this revision of the tariff takes place it must be the result of careful investigation and consideration and after the opinion of experts has been had in every department of trade. But, because disaster has overtaken men who have engaged in stock speculation, and men who have floated fictitious enterprises on the public it is no reason why the government should go to the rescue and disarrange the financial and industrial affairs of the country-

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this discussion was brought about by the introduction of a resolution by the bon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Borden, Halifax) asking that further consideration in the way of increased duties be given to the steel industries of Canada. It was met, first, by the reply from the hon. Minister of Finance (Hon. Mr. Fielding) that it was not an opportune moment at which to bring forward this resolution intimating that it was unfair that my hon. friend should have brought this resolution forward at this particular time. He did not give us any reason for making this statement, but thought that this House should be satisfied with the fact that he simply made the bald assertion that it was untimely. At the beginning of this session, or nearly at the
beginning of this session, when the budget speech was delivered by the hon. Minister of Finance, a resolution was proposed by my hon. friend in which he declared, and in which those supporting him declared, that the hour for the revision of the tariff had arrived in this country. It was voted down and there has never been any moment since that time when we were going into Committee of Supply that it was not the legitimate right of the hon. leader of the opposition, or of any hon. gentleman on this side of the House, to move such a resolution as that which was moved today. So, Sir, I say that it does not become the hon. Minister of Finance to put forth that as the basis of his argument against the introduction of his resolution. It indicates fear, it indicates cowardice on the part of the hon. gentleman when he attempts to ward off the pressure that is brought to bear on him from all sorts of financial institutions throughout Canada ; it ill becomes him to say in a whining manner to the leader of the opposition that this motion is inopportune. But we have a franker statement from the Prime Minister who told us that it could not be expected that the government would revise the irom tariff without first having a statement from the Sydney Company. Well, to a protectionist like myself, a protectionist in season and out of season, who believes in the application of principles rather than dodging between two theories, it does seem peculiar that the leader of the government should have to wait to apply his sound principles until he inspects the private books of a company. The right hon. gentleman told us that the growth of this industry had been brought about by the tariff inaugurated by his government, which is lower than the tariff of the Conservative government. If that is true, then for heaven's sake do not let the hon. gentleman return to a higher tariff and ruin the industry. But the Prime Minister, in the next breath, told us that he was going to look oyer the books of that concern, and that if he finds good reason for returning to higher protection he will do so. That is the kind of shifting policy we have had for six years of Liberal rule in Canada, and it is a sort of policy that has never built up industrial life in any country. The Liberals have been lucky. Since they came to power they have had the benefit of prosperous times and wonderful crops, but, notwithstanding that, they are now beginning to learn that they made a mistake when they did not revise the tariff this year. It is quite true that if they once open the door they will have many other industries knocking ; they will find the silver lead men of British Columbia and others demanding protection, and I can well understand how they are in fear and trembling. But, Sir, no government, whether free trade or revenue tariff, or protectionist, can sit supinely there and permit such a

great industry as that at Sydney to go to the wall. If the prayers of the men interested in that industry have any foundation, the government will be bound to increase the iron duties and to declare to all Canada within thirty days that the leader of the opposition is really the leader of the House. They may dislike to do so. They may get their supporters to bob up here and there, one after another to declare that they are in sympathy with the motion, but will vote against it, but all their hedging won't do. The only man who is in sympathy with the motion is the man who has the moral courage to vote for the motion when it embodies the principle he believes in. And now as to stock gambling. We are not concerned about that on this side of the House. Pei

haps we do not deal in stocks as extensively as hon. gentlemen opposite do. I noticed that when the hon. member for Labelle suggested an investigation, many gentlemen opposite applauded, and I thought at once that these gentlemen had dropped their money, and even though an investigation could not find out where it went to, it would give them some consolation. They want consolation instead of cash, and if the iron industry is not protected that is all the people of Canada will get. I have listened to the Finance Minister, I have listened to the Prime Minister, I have listened to the Minister of Customs, the thunderer of the administration, quoting stock prices in this country and in this House as an evidence of prosperity. Why are they ashamed to quote those stock lists to-nightV For several years we have heard the Liberals glory that they established the works at Sydney. Where is their glorification tonight ? I do not care whether the management of these works has been extravagant or not. I never knew of a new industry of such an extensive nature that did not commit mistakes. It is not enough to have markets for their products and to have their raw material, but you must have practiced and experienced men to mould the iron from its raw state into its perfect manufactured condition. That man has to grow up in the institution, and that is one of the great reasons why protection must be had in a new country with infant industries. Now, Sir, what sympathy are hon. gentlemen opposite showing to these men who are said to be in difficulty-saying that there should be a committee to investigate the heads of the company-Mr. Cox, Mr. Boss and others who but a year ago they were lauding to the skies ? As Liberals, they were at that time gloating over the fact that they were establishing a great industry down by the sea. To-day they are characterizing these men as great stock gamblers who should not receive any protection. Great is the ehange that has come over hon. gentlemen opposite and over this great industry down by the sea.

The statute does not expressly forbid it, but it was expressly declared in this House when the statute was passed, that its object was. to make provision for the return of superannuation money to men who were dismissed for political offences. The ground we took was that while these men have been punished by losing their office, they should not be further penalized by the loss of their superannuation money. I do not think that is what the country expects or what the country was promised. It has been the boast of the right hon. If the minister wants legal assistance, he has at his command at all times his friend the Minister of Justice, who I am sure is well qualified to advise him on legal questions. I do think it is a slight upon the great agricultural community of this country that the Department of Agriculture here at Ottawa should be filled up with professional men who know nothing about practical agriculture. I know nothing of the gentleman who occupies the position in question.
